title: Aurivan CISA Topic Notes
source: Original Aurivan study notes, organized by the 2024 CISA exam content outline. Not affiliated with or endorsed by ISACA.
description: Plain-language notes for every topic in the CISA exam outline: what each idea means, how ISACA expects you to think about it, and the traps to avoid.

domains.summary: This domain is about how an IS audit is run from start to finish: the professional rules and mandate behind it, choosing what to audit based on risk, understanding controls, testing and sampling, gathering evidence, using data analytics, reporting results, and keeping audit quality high. It is the method behind every other domain.
domains.real_life_analogy: An IS audit works like an independent home inspection. The inspector is engaged under clear terms (the audit charter) and must not be the builder who did the work (independence). Because time is limited, they focus on the riskiest areas, such as wiring and the roof (risk-based planning), test a sample of outlets rather than every one (sampling), and trust what they measure themselves over what the seller tells them (evidence reliability). Their report rates each defect and recommends fixes, but the owner decides what to repair (management decides). A follow-up visit confirms the repairs were actually made.

topics.topic_name: IS Audit Standards, Guidelines, Functions, and Codes of Ethics
topics.summary: The rulebook and the reporting line. Before any testing starts, the auditor needs a mandate, a set of professional rules, and the freedom to report honestly.

subtopics.name: ITAF: Standards, Guidelines, and Tools and Techniques
subtopics.summary: ISACA groups its professional rules for IS auditors into one framework with three layers. The top layer is required; the middle layer explains how to meet it; the bottom layer offers ready-made examples you adapt. Think of a driving test: the traffic laws are compulsory, the instructor's advice is strongly recommended, and the practice routes are just samples. Precise term: the IT Audit Framework (ITAF), made up of mandatory Standards, advisory Guidelines, and informational Tools and Techniques.

categories.Standards: Mandatory. Cover general matters (such as independence and proficiency), performance (such as planning and evidence) and reporting.
categories.Guidelines: Advisory. Explain how to apply a standard; departures must be justifiable.
categories.Tools and techniques: Informational. Example audit programs, checklists and white papers that must be tailored to each engagement.

subtopics.key_point: Standards are minimum requirements and cannot be set aside. Guidelines are not mandatory, but the auditor must consider them and be ready to justify any departure.

subtopics.exam_tip: A common trap treats a guideline as optional to ignore without explanation, or treats a standard as something you can depart from with good documentation. Only guidelines allow a justified departure.

subtopics.name: The Audit Charter
subtopics.summary: Every audit function needs written permission to exist and to look where it must. That permission comes from a short document approved above the people being audited. If the auditee's own management approves it, the auditor ends up working for the people under review. Precise term: the audit charter, the board- or audit-committee-approved document that sets the IS audit function's purpose, authority, responsibility, scope and reporting line.
subtopics.key_point: The charter is approved by the board or audit committee, never by auditee management such as the CIO or CFO. Who approves it decides whether the function is independent.
common_mistakes: Thinking a CIO sign-off is enough because the CIO owns IT.
Expecting the charter to list specific audit subjects or dates.
subtopics.exam_tip: Do not confuse the charter with the annual audit plan. The charter sets authority and rarely changes; the list of audits for the year belongs in the risk-based plan.

subtopics.name: Independence and Objectivity
subtopics.summary: An auditor's opinion is only worth something if nobody can say it was bent. Independence is about the structure: whom the audit function reports to. Objectivity is about the person: whether this auditor has a reason to go easy. Precise terms: organizational independence (functional reporting to the audit committee) and individual objectivity, protected by managing threats such as self-review, self-interest and familiarity.

categories.Self-review threat: Auditing your own earlier work, such as a system you helped design.
categories.Self-interest threat: A personal stake in the result, such as a job offer from the auditee.
categories.Familiarity threat: Long tenure on the same area; the usual safeguard is rotation.
categories.Undue pressure: Management trying to soften or remove findings; escalate to the audit committee.

subtopics.key_point: Remove a serious threat rather than merely disclose it. An auditor who designed a system, or who has accepted a future job at the auditee, is reassigned; a minor threat may be handled with disclosure and safeguards.

illustration.caption: Reporting lines and independence. A functional line to the audit committee protects it; a line to an executive who controls the audit budget weakens it.

subtopics.exam_tip: Watch for reporting lines that run through the CFO or CIO who also control the audit budget. The fix is functional reporting to the audit committee.

subtopics.name: The IS Audit Function and the Audit Committee
subtopics.summary: Inside an organization, the audit team is a permanent function, not a one-off project. It needs enough skilled people, a plan, supervision and quality checks, scaled to the organization's size and risk. The audit committee is a board group of independent directors that oversees the auditors and receives their reports. Precise term: the internal IS audit function, governed through the audit committee's oversight.
subtopics.key_point: The audit committee protects audit independence. When management pressures the auditor to drop or soften findings, the auditor escalates to the audit committee.
common_mistakes: Assuming a small audit team can skip supervision or quality monitoring.
Letting the function's own budget holder decide what gets audited.
subtopics.exam_tip: When internal and external auditors work together, each keeps its own reporting line. Coordination avoids duplication; it never merges their independence.

subtopics.name: ISACA Code of Professional Ethics
subtopics.summary: Members and certification holders agree to a short code of conduct. In plain terms: support good governance, act honestly and carefully, keep confidential information private, stay competent, tell the right people everything significant you found, and help the profession grow. Precise term: the ISACA Code of Professional Ethics, which can lead to disciplinary action if breached.

categories.Governance: Support appropriate standards and controls for information systems.
categories.Due care: Work objectively, diligently and to professional standards.
categories.Legality: Serve stakeholders lawfully and keep high standards of conduct.
categories.Confidentiality: Protect information gained at work and do not use it for personal gain.
categories.Competence: Take on only work you can do competently and keep skills current.
categories.Disclosure: Tell appropriate parties the results of work, including all significant facts.
categories.Professional development: Help stakeholders understand IS and help the profession grow.

subtopics.key_point: Disclosing all significant facts is a duty. Leaving out a finding because of pressure or an inducement breaches the code.
subtopics.exam_tip: Confidentiality does not mean hiding things from the people entitled to know. It means not disclosing information outside proper channels, unless law requires it.

subtopics.name: Other Professional Standards and Conflicts
subtopics.summary: Many auditors work under more than one rulebook, such as ISACA's ITAF and the internal-audit standards of the Institute of Internal Auditors. Usually they agree. When they differ on a point, you need a rule for which one wins. Precise term: applying the more rigorous requirement, which satisfies both sets of standards.
subtopics.key_point: If two committed standards differ, follow the stricter one and document the difference. That choice complies with both.
subtopics.exam_tip: The trap is picking the easier or the 'local' standard because it is quicker. The stricter rule is the safe answer.

topics.topic_name: Types of Audits, Assessments, and Reviews
topics.summary: Not every review gives the same comfort. Learn what each engagement type promises, so you can tell assurance from advice.

subtopics.name: Audit Types by Objective
subtopics.summary: Audits are named after what they check. A compliance audit asks whether rules are followed; an operational audit asks whether work is efficient and effective; a financial audit asks whether the numbers are fairly stated; an IS audit asks whether systems and data are properly controlled. Precise term: engagement types defined by their objective and the criteria they test against.

categories.Compliance: Conformity with laws, regulations, policies or contracts.
categories.Operational: Efficiency and effectiveness of a process.
categories.IS / IT: Controls over systems, infrastructure and data.
categories.Forensic: Gathering evidence of suspected fraud or wrongdoing for possible legal use.
categories.Specialized / third party: Reviews of service providers, such as SOC reports.

subtopics.key_point: Pick the audit type from the objective and criteria. If the criteria are laws, regulations or contracts, it is a compliance audit.
subtopics.exam_tip: Do not confuse an operational audit (efficiency and effectiveness) with a compliance audit (conformity with rules). The stem's criteria give it away.

subtopics.name: Assurance, Advisory, and Agreed-Upon Procedures
subtopics.summary: Some engagements end with an opinion you can rely on; others do not. An assurance engagement tests against criteria and concludes. An advisory engagement helps management improve something. An agreed-upon procedures engagement just runs the steps the client chose and reports the facts. Precise terms: assurance (opinion or conclusion), consulting/advisory (recommendations), and agreed-upon procedures (factual findings, no opinion).
subtopics.key_point: Agree the engagement type, scope and limits up front. Advisory work on a control the function later audits creates a self-review threat that needs disclosure and safeguards.
subtopics.exam_tip: An agreed-upon procedures report gives no assurance. If an answer says it 'confirms the controls are effective', it is wrong.

subtopics.name: Readiness and Maturity Assessments
subtopics.summary: Before a formal audit, an organization may ask, 'Are we ready?' or 'How mature are we?' A readiness review looks at whether controls are designed sensibly. A maturity assessment rates how capable a process is against a model. Neither one tests whether controls actually worked over a period. Precise terms: readiness assessment and capability or maturity assessment, both distinct from an assurance audit.
subtopics.key_point: Only an assurance audit, which tests operating effectiveness, provides assurance. A maturity rating is a measure of capability, not proof that controls operate.

illustration.caption: A readiness review looks only at control design. A formal audit goes further and tests whether the controls operate.

subtopics.exam_tip: A high maturity score is a tempting wrong answer when the question asks for evidence that controls work.

subtopics.name: Service Organization (SOC) Reports
subtopics.summary: When a company outsources a service, its auditors cannot always visit the provider. Instead they read a report from the provider's independent auditor. These reports differ in focus and depth. Precise terms: SOC 1 (controls relevant to customers' financial reporting), SOC 2 (Trust Services Criteria such as security and availability), SOC 3 (a public summary of SOC 2); Type 1 (design at a point in time) and Type 2 (design plus operating effectiveness over a period).

categories.SOC 2: Security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy.
categories.Type 1: Design at a point in time.
categories.Type 2: Design and operating effectiveness over a period.

subtopics.key_point: To rely on a provider's controls over a period, you need a Type 2 report. Check the period, the scope, any exceptions, and the controls the customer must operate itself.
subtopics.exam_tip: Under the carve-out method, a subservice provider's controls are excluded from the report. The user auditor still needs separate assurance over them.

subtopics.name: Control Self-Assessment (CSA)
subtopics.summary: In a CSA, the people who run a process meet, usually in a facilitated workshop, and judge their own controls. The auditor guides the discussion rather than doing the testing. It builds ownership and spreads control awareness. Precise term: control self-assessment, a management-owned technique that the audit function may facilitate.

categories.Benefits: Earlier detection of risk, stronger ownership, better communication, more coverage with limited audit staff.
categories.Limits: Self-reports can be optimistic; results must be checked against actual outcomes.

subtopics.key_point: CSA complements independent audit work; it never replaces it. Audit conclusions still rest on the auditor's own procedures.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 108' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Control self-assessment: staff and management assess their own controls; the IS auditor facilitates'><rect x='14' y='28' width='206' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='117' y='54' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Staff assess controls</text><rect x='246' y='28' width='200' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='346' y='54' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>IS auditor facilitates</text><text x='117' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>they own the controls</text><text x='346' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>guides, does not test</text></svg>
illustration.caption: In a control self-assessment, the process owners judge their own controls. The auditor facilitates and does not test.

subtopics.exam_tip: A good facilitator draws out the group's view and records dissent. Steering participants toward the auditor's preferred answer defeats the purpose.

subtopics.name: Integrated Audits
subtopics.summary: IT controls and business processes are tangled together: a payment can only be right if both the system and the people around it work. An integrated audit looks at both in one engagement so nothing falls through the gap between separate teams. Precise term: integrated auditing, which combines IT, financial and operational audit work into one risk-based engagement and report.
subtopics.key_point: The main reason to integrate is interdependence. Weak IT general controls reduce reliance on automated controls and push the auditor toward more substantive testing.

illustration.caption: Integrated auditing. IT, financial and operational work come together in a single engagement and one report.

subtopics.exam_tip: An integrated report links each IT weakness to its business or financial effect. A report that lists IT issues without business impact is not truly integrated.

topics.summary: Audit time is limited, so spend it where things are most likely to go wrong and would hurt most.

subtopics.name: The Audit Universe and the Annual Plan
subtopics.summary: Start with a full list of everything that could be audited: systems, processes, locations, vendors and shared services. Then rank them by risk and choose what to cover this cycle. If something is missing from the list, it can never be chosen. Precise terms: the audit universe (the complete catalog of auditable entities) and the risk-based audit plan built from it.
subtopics.key_point: Rank audit subjects by current risk, refreshed every cycle, not by rotation, habit or convenience. A complete universe comes first.
subtopics.exam_tip: If resources fall or a major incident happens mid-year, re-prioritize by risk, document the change and tell the audit committee. Quietly dropping audits is the trap.

subtopics.name: Planning an Individual Engagement
subtopics.summary: Each audit follows the same opening moves: learn the business, identify the risks, set objectives, then define scope and approach, and finally line up the people with the right skills. Scope follows risk; you do not choose scope first and look for risk afterwards. Precise terms: audit objectives (what the audit must determine) and audit scope (the boundaries of systems, locations and periods covered).
subtopics.key_point: Every scope item, procedure and conclusion should trace back to an objective, and every objective back to a risk.

illustration.caption: Planning one audit. Understanding the business and analyzing risk come before scope is set.

subtopics.exam_tip: Maximum coverage is not a good scope. A scope that tries to test everything usually ignores the risks that matter.

subtopics.name: Risk Assessment Methods
subtopics.summary: To rank risks, you combine how likely something is with how bad it would be, then allow for the controls already in place. You can do this with words (high, medium, low) or with numbers (expected loss). Precise terms: qualitative and quantitative risk assessment, often using a likelihood-impact matrix or heat map.
subtopics.key_point: Choose the method that fits the data. Use numbers where reliable history exists; use defined qualitative scales where it does not, so different people rate consistently.
common_mistakes: Using a qualitative scale with no definitions, so every rater means something different.
Never updating the assessment after an acquisition, new regulation or major incident.
subtopics.exam_tip: Ranking on impact alone, or likelihood alone, is a trap. Both dimensions count, adjusted for existing controls.

subtopics.name: Audit Risk and Its Three Parts
subtopics.summary: Audit risk is the chance the auditor signs off on something that is actually wrong. Part of it comes from the business itself, part from weak controls, and part from the auditor's own testing missing the problem. Only the last part is in the auditor's hands. Precise terms: inherent risk, control risk and detection risk, where audit risk = inherent risk x control risk x detection risk.
subtopics.key_point: The auditor manages audit risk by adjusting detection risk, through the nature, timing and extent of testing. When inherent and control risk are high, detection risk must be low, so testing increases.

subtopics.name: Materiality
subtopics.summary: Not every error matters equally. Something is material if it could change the decisions of the people who rely on the audit. Size counts, but so do nature and context: a small error that hides a fraud or breaks a law can still be material. Precise term: materiality, judged on quantitative and qualitative factors.
subtopics.key_point: Judge materiality in aggregate and in context, including how much other controls depend on the failing one. Small individual errors can add up to a material problem.
subtopics.exam_tip: The trap is judging only by the average amount per item. Volume, sensitivity and regulatory exposure also count.

subtopics.name: Laws, Regulations, and the Audit Plan
subtopics.summary: Rules from outside the organization shape what must be audited and how often. The auditor needs to know which laws apply and what they require, but is not the organization's lawyer. Precise term: the effect of laws and regulations on IS audit planning.
subtopics.key_point: Understand regulatory requirements for planning, and rely on legal and compliance specialists for interpretation. Where several regimes apply, evaluate each one's requirements explicitly.
subtopics.exam_tip: Assuming one regime's compliance covers another is a trap. Map the requirements and look for gaps.

topics.summary: Controls are how management keeps risk inside acceptable limits. The auditor's job is to judge whether they are designed well and actually work.

subtopics.name: Internal Control Basics
subtopics.summary: Internal controls are the policies, procedures, practices and structures that help an organization meet its goals and avoid trouble. They can never be perfect: people make mistakes, collude, or override them, and every control has a cost. Precise term: internal control, which provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance over operations, reporting and compliance.

categories.Control environment: The tone and culture that underpin every other control.
categories.Risk assessment: Identifying what could stop objectives being met.
categories.Control activities: The specific checks, approvals and restrictions.
categories.Information and communication: Getting the right information to the right people.
categories.Monitoring: Ongoing and separate evaluations of whether controls still work.

subtopics.key_point: Controls give reasonable assurance only. Collusion and management override are inherent limitations, so detective controls are layered on top of preventive ones.
subtopics.exam_tip: Any option promising that a control 'guarantees' or 'eliminates' a risk is almost always wrong.

subtopics.name: Preventive, Detective, and Corrective Controls
subtopics.summary: One useful way to sort controls is by when they act. Some stop a problem before it happens, some spot it after it has occurred, and some fix the damage. Strong control design uses a mix. Precise terms: preventive, detective and corrective controls (some sources add deterrent, compensating and recovery).
subtopics.key_point: Preventive is usually preferred because stopping an event is cheaper than cleaning it up, but detective controls are still needed because no prevention is perfect.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 520 138' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Control timing: preventive controls act before an incident, detective controls as it happens, corrective controls after'><line x1='174' y1='28' x2='174' y2='106' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='174' y='22' text-anchor='middle' font-family='JetBrains Mono, monospace' font-size='7.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--accent-fill)' letter-spacing='0.08em'>INCIDENT</text><rect x='14' y='44' width='150' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='89' y='70' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Preventive</text><rect x='185' y='44' width='150' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='260' y='70' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Detective</text><rect x='356' y='44' width='150' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='431' y='70' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Corrective</text><line x1='14' y1='104' x2='499' y2='104' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M499,100 L506,104 L499,108 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><text x='89' y='124' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>stop it before</text><text x='260' y='124' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>spot it once it occurs</text><text x='431' y='124' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>fix the damage after</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Sorting controls by timing. Most risks are covered by all three types working together.

subtopics.exam_tip: Classify by function, not by technology. A log is detective only if someone reviews it; a backup is corrective because it restores after the event.

subtopics.name: General IT Controls and Application Controls
subtopics.summary: Some controls protect the whole IT environment, like who can change programs or log in to servers. Others live inside one application, like a field that rejects an invalid date. The broad controls must work for the narrow ones to be trusted. Precise terms: IT general controls (ITGCs) such as access, change management and operations; and application controls such as input, processing and output checks.

categories.IT general controls: Logical access, change management, IT operations, backup and recovery.
categories.Application controls: Input validation, processing checks, output reconciliation.

subtopics.key_point: If IT general controls fail, automated application controls cannot be relied on, because someone could have changed them unnoticed.
subtopics.exam_tip: Change management needs authorization, testing, approval and separation between the people who build a change and those who move it to production.

subtopics.name: Control Objectives and Control Measures
subtopics.summary: A control objective is the result you want, such as 'only authorized changes reach production'. A control measure is the specific mechanism that achieves it, such as a change approval workflow. Good objectives are specific, testable and linked to a risk or a rule. Precise terms: control objective versus control (measure or activity).
subtopics.key_point: Test against the objective. A control that runs perfectly but does not address the objective's risk adds little.
subtopics.exam_tip: Do not confuse the goal with the tool. 'Ensure data integrity' is an objective; 'reconcile batch totals' is a control.

subtopics.name: Compensating Controls and Defense in Depth
subtopics.summary: When an ideal control is impractical, such as full segregation of duties in a tiny team, another control can reduce the same risk a different way, often an independent review. Layers of controls together cover more failure modes. Precise terms: compensating control and defense in depth.
subtopics.key_point: A compensating control only works if it is truly independent. A person reviewing their own work is not a compensating control.
common_mistakes: Counting controls instead of mapping them to failure modes.
Accepting a 'review' performed by the same person who did the work.
subtopics.exam_tip: Judge layered controls by whether together they cover each way things can fail, not by how many layers there are.

subtopics.name: Controls, Inherent Risk, and Residual Risk
subtopics.summary: Risk before any controls is inherent risk. Controls shrink it, and what is left is residual risk. Residual risk almost never reaches zero, so management must decide whether to accept it. Precise terms: inherent risk, residual risk and risk acceptance.
subtopics.key_point: Accepting residual risk is a management decision. The auditor evaluates and recommends; management decides and owns the risk.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Controls reduce inherent risk to a smaller residual risk that remains'><rect x='14' y='38' width='130' height='46' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='79' y='65' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Inherent risk</text><rect x='174' y='38' width='112' height='46' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='230' y='65' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Controls</text><rect x='316' y='38' width='130' height='46' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='381' y='65' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Residual risk</text><line x1='146' y1='61' x2='165' y2='61' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M165,57 L172,61 L165,65 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='288' y1='61' x2='307' y2='61' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M307,57 L314,61 L307,65 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><text x='79' y='104' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>risk before controls</text><text x='230' y='104' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>what they remove</text><text x='381' y='104' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>the risk that remains</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Controls bring inherent risk down to residual risk. Some risk remains, and management decides whether to accept it.

subtopics.exam_tip: An auditor who 'accepts the risk on behalf of the business' is a classic wrong answer.

subtopics.name: Control Monitoring and the Control Environment
subtopics.summary: Management should watch its own controls continuously, for example by reviewing exception reports. Separately, independent evaluators such as internal audit check those controls periodically. Both rest on the culture: if staff are afraid to report problems, well-written controls fail. Precise terms: ongoing (management) monitoring, separate (independent) evaluations, and the control environment.
subtopics.key_point: Management monitoring and independent audit are complementary. Audit can rely on management's monitoring only after testing it.
subtopics.exam_tip: If management's self-assessment missed failures the auditor found, that gap is a separate finding about monitoring effectiveness.

topics.summary: An audit is a project with a goal, a budget, a team and a deadline. Running it well is what turns good planning into reliable conclusions.

subtopics.name: Audit Phases
subtopics.summary: Most audits move through the same stages: plan the work, carry out fieldwork, report the results, then follow up. Planning depth should match the risk and complexity of the subject. During fieldwork, supervisors review evidence as it comes in and record any change to the plan. Precise terms: planning, fieldwork (execution), reporting and follow-up phases.
subtopics.key_point: If major new facts appear mid-engagement that undermine the audit, pause, document and let the audit committee decide how to proceed.
subtopics.exam_tip: Reopening fieldwork during reporting to chase new issues, or letting management rewrite the report, are both traps. Reporting validates facts and finalizes conclusions.

subtopics.name: Audit Programs
subtopics.summary: An audit program is the step-by-step list of procedures for an engagement. It tells the team what to test and how, gives supervisors something to review against, and becomes a record of what was done. Precise term: audit program, the documented set of procedures designed to meet the audit objectives.
subtopics.key_point: Every procedure should serve an objective. Templates are adapted to the engagement's risks, and the program is updated, with approval, when fieldwork reveals significant risks it does not cover.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 458 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='An audit program links audit objectives to procedures, the evidence they gather, and the conclusion'><rect x='8' y='24' width='110' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='63' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Audit objective</text><rect x='140' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='186' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Procedures</text><rect x='254' y='24' width='82' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='295' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Evidence</text><rect x='358' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='404' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Conclusion</text><line x1='120' y1='46' x2='131' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M131,42 L138,46 L131,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='234' y1='46' x2='245' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M245,42 L252,46 L245,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='338' y1='46' x2='349' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M349,42 L356,46 L349,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: An audit program connects each objective to the procedures that gather evidence for a conclusion.

subtopics.exam_tip: Running a generic template unchanged is a trap. So is changing the program on the fly without approval or documentation.

subtopics.name: Resources, Skills, and Budgets
subtopics.summary: An audit needs the right people with the right skills when it runs. If the team lacks a skill, such as cloud security or forensics, the gap is closed before or during the engagement. Precise terms: proficiency, co-sourcing and use of experts.
subtopics.key_point: Close competency gaps with training, specialists or co-sourcing, but the auditor keeps responsibility for the conclusions. When budgets shrink, reallocate by risk and disclose any reduction in scope.
subtopics.exam_tip: Before relying on an expert, assess their competence and objectivity and evaluate the work they deliver. Checking credentials alone is not enough.

subtopics.name: Work Papers and Documentation
subtopics.summary: Work papers are the audit's memory. They show what was planned, what was done, what evidence was found and how each conclusion was reached, so another experienced auditor could follow the trail. Precise term: audit documentation (work papers), with cross-references linking findings, procedures and evidence.
subtopics.key_point: Documentation must let a reviewer trace every conclusion back to sufficient, appropriate evidence. It is retained for the required period and protected from unauthorized change or access.
subtopics.exam_tip: A litigation hold overrides routine deletion schedules. Relevant documentation is preserved and scope is agreed with legal counsel.

subtopics.name: Agile Auditing
subtopics.summary: Instead of one long audit with a single report at the end, an agile audit works in short cycles. Each cycle delivers some results, and the team adjusts what comes next based on what it learned. Precise term: agile auditing, using sprints, regular stakeholder feedback and retrospectives.
subtopics.key_point: Agile auditing suits fast-changing subjects and stakeholders who want frequent, incremental assurance. Lessons from each retrospective feed the next sprint's plan.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='A traditional audit runs as one long linear pass; an agile audit runs in short iterative cycles'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Traditional audit</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>One long linear pass</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Agile audit</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Short iterative cycles</text></svg>
illustration.caption: A traditional audit is one long pass. An agile audit runs short cycles and adjusts as it learns.

subtopics.exam_tip: Agile does not mean less rigor. Standards on evidence, documentation and independence still apply in every sprint.

topics.summary: You can rarely check everything. Testing and sampling let you reach a defensible conclusion from a well-chosen part.

subtopics.name: Compliance Testing versus Substantive Testing
subtopics.summary: There are two big questions an auditor asks. First: is the control working? Second: is the data itself right? The first is answered by testing controls, the second by testing the transactions or balances directly. Precise terms: compliance (control) testing and substantive testing.
subtopics.key_point: The results of compliance testing decide how much substantive testing is needed. Weak controls mean more substantive work; strong controls allow less, but not none.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Compliance testing checks whether a control operates; substantive testing checks whether the data is accurate'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Compliance</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Does the control operate?</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Substantive</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Is the data accurate?</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Compliance testing asks whether the control works. Substantive testing asks whether the data is right.

subtopics.exam_tip: Controls tested at an interim date need roll-forward evidence for the rest of the period before you rely on them.

subtopics.name: Statistical and Non-Statistical Sampling
subtopics.summary: Sampling means testing part of a population to conclude about the whole. If the items are chosen randomly and the math is planned, you can say how confident you are. If the auditor hand-picks items, you learn something useful but cannot project it mathematically. Precise terms: statistical sampling and judgmental (non-statistical) sampling.
subtopics.key_point: When a stated confidence level is required, use statistical sampling. A sample only supports conclusions about the population it was drawn from, so define that population and check its completeness first.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Statistical sampling projects to the population with quantifiable confidence; judgmental sampling cannot be projected'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Statistical</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Projects to the population</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Judgmental</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Cannot be projected</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Only a statistical sample can be projected to the whole population with measurable confidence.

subtopics.exam_tip: Zero-tolerance populations, such as privileged access to payment systems, may need 100 percent testing rather than a sample.

subtopics.name: Attribute, Variable, and Discovery Sampling
subtopics.summary: What you are measuring decides the method. Counting how often a control fails is different from estimating how many dollars are wrong. Precise terms: attribute sampling (deviation rates, for control tests), variable sampling (amounts, for substantive tests), and discovery sampling (finding at least one occurrence when fraud or critical errors are suspected).

categories.Attribute: Yes/no result per item; estimates a deviation rate.
categories.Discovery: Designed to find at least one example if the rate exceeds a threshold.
categories.Stop-or-go: Lets the auditor stop early if few errors are found.

subtopics.key_point: Match the method to the objective: attribute for controls, variable for amounts, discovery when one occurrence matters.
subtopics.exam_tip: Mixing them up is the main trap. A question about a control's failure rate never wants a dollar-value method.

subtopics.name: Selection Methods: Random, Systematic, Stratified, Monetary-Unit
subtopics.summary: Once you know what to measure, you choose how to pick items. Random selection gives each item an equal chance, and systematic selection takes every nth item after a random start. Stratified selection samples each subgroup separately, while monetary-unit selection gives larger amounts a bigger chance of being picked. Precise terms: random, systematic, stratified and monetary-unit sampling (MUS).
subtopics.key_point: Use stratification when subgroups behave differently; it is more efficient and supports conclusions per group. Use MUS when the goal is to estimate dollar misstatement.
common_mistakes: Using a systematic interval on a population with a repeating pattern.
Assuming a huge population needs a proportionally huge sample.
subtopics.exam_tip: MUS under-represents small and zero-value items, so it is a poor fit for finding understatements.

subtopics.name: Sample Size and Sampling Risk
subtopics.summary: Sample size grows when you want more confidence, when you expect more errors, and when you can tolerate fewer. Population size has surprisingly little effect once it is large. Even a good sample can mislead, which is sampling risk. Precise terms: confidence level, tolerable deviation rate, expected deviation rate, and the risks of incorrect acceptance (overreliance) and incorrect rejection.
subtopics.key_point: Overreliance, concluding a control works when it does not, is the more dangerous error because it gives false assurance.
subtopics.exam_tip: If the sample deviation rate clearly exceeds the tolerable rate, do not rely on the control. If it falls in between, extend or redesign the sample before concluding.

topics.summary: Conclusions are only as good as the evidence behind them. Know which techniques produce strong evidence and which only produce claims.

subtopics.name: Sufficient and Appropriate Evidence
subtopics.summary: Evidence has two tests. Is there enough of it? And is it good enough: does it actually relate to the question, and can it be trusted? Precise terms: sufficiency (quantity) and appropriateness (quality, made up of relevance and reliability).
subtopics.key_point: More evidence cannot fix poor-quality evidence. A pile of unreliable documents is still unreliable.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Audit evidence must be sufficient, meaning enough of it, and appropriate, meaning relevant and reliable'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='119' y='36' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Sufficient</text><text x='119' y='51' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='600' fill='#ffffff'>enough of it (quantity)</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='341' y='36' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Appropriate</text><text x='341' y='51' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='600' fill='#ffffff'>good enough (quality)</text><line x1='341' y1='60' x2='290' y2='88' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='341' y1='60' x2='392' y2='88' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='236' y='88' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='286' y='114' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Relevant</text><rect x='346' y='88' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='396' y='114' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Reliable</text></svg>
illustration.caption: The two tests of audit evidence. Sufficiency is about quantity; appropriateness is about quality, which means relevant and reliable.

subtopics.exam_tip: Read the question for which test is failing. 'Too few items' is sufficiency; 'from the wrong source' is reliability; 'about a different control' is relevance.

subtopics.name: Evidence Techniques and Their Reliability
subtopics.summary: Auditors gather evidence by asking (inquiry and interviews), looking (observation and inspection), redoing (reperformance), asking outsiders (confirmation) and analyzing data. Some sources are much stronger than others. Precise term: the evidence reliability hierarchy.

categories.Strongest: Auditor reperformance, direct observation, independent third-party confirmation.
categories.Middle: Documents and system records produced by the auditee under good controls.
categories.Weakest: Verbal statements and management representations alone.

subtopics.key_point: Evidence the auditor obtains directly, such as reperformance or observation, is stronger than what the auditee tells or gives you. Independent outside sources beat internal ones, and inquiry alone is never enough.
subtopics.exam_tip: Reperformance today shows how a process works now, not what happened months ago. For past events, contemporaneous system records are better.

subtopics.name: Interviews and Observation
subtopics.summary: Talking to people and watching them work shows how controls really run, not just how the policy says they should. Good interviews are prepared, use open questions and involve careful listening. Precise term: inquiry and observation, which usually need corroboration with other evidence.
subtopics.key_point: Use interviews to understand and to find leads, then corroborate with documents, data or reperformance before concluding.
subtopics.exam_tip: Observation only proves what happened while you watched. People often behave differently when observed.

subtopics.name: Electronic and System-Generated Evidence
subtopics.summary: Much evidence now comes out of systems: reports, logs, extracts. A report can look official and still be incomplete or wrong. Precise terms: completeness and accuracy of information produced by the entity, and integrity controls such as hashing.
subtopics.key_point: Before relying on a system report, establish that it is complete and accurate, by testing the controls that generate it or reproducing it independently.
subtopics.exam_tip: Capture electronic evidence in a controlled way, verify it has not changed (for example with a hash) and document the chain from source to work paper.

subtopics.name: Handling Suspected Fraud
subtopics.summary: Sometimes an audit uncovers signs of fraud: a person who never takes leave, unusual overrides, missing approvals. Fraud usually needs pressure, an opportunity and a way to rationalize it. The auditor's job is to notice and escalate, not to become an investigator alone. Precise terms: the fraud triangle, fraud indicators (red flags), and chain of custody.
subtopics.key_point: On finding fraud indicators, document the facts and escalate through the organization's fraud-response procedure. Do not confront the suspect or investigate alone.
common_mistakes: Interviewing the suspect alone without contemporaneous notes.
Alerting the suspect before evidence is secured.
subtopics.exam_tip: If the case may go to court, preserve evidence with a documented chain of custody. When forensic skills are needed, specialists are engaged and the auditor supports and coordinates.

topics.summary: Technology lets the auditor test whole populations, watch transactions as they happen, and spot patterns no person could see. It also brings new risks to manage.

subtopics.name: Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques (CAATs)
subtopics.summary: CAATs are tools and methods that let the auditor use a computer to test data. Instead of picking 25 invoices by hand, you can run a query over every invoice and list the duplicates. Precise terms: computer-assisted audit techniques, including generalized audit software (GAS) for querying data extracts, and test data or an integrated test facility (ITF) for testing program logic.

categories.Generalized audit software: Independent queries over full data extracts.
categories.Test data: Auditor-prepared transactions run through a program to check its logic.
categories.Integrated test facility: Dummy entity inside the live system; compares actual and expected results.
categories.Embedded audit modules: Code inside the application that flags transactions as they process.

subtopics.key_point: Run CAATs on read-only copies or extracts so production is protected and the auditor controls the procedure. CAATs add most value with large volumes, full-population tests and pattern detection.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Manual testing covers a sample of transactions; CAATs test the entire population'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Manual testing</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>A sample of transactions</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>CAATs</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Tests 100% of transactions</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Manual testing looks at a sample. CAATs can test every transaction in the population.

subtopics.exam_tip: An ITF pushes fictitious transactions through the live system, so those test entries must be isolated and reversed. GAS, by contrast, analyzes data that already exists.

subtopics.name: Continuous Auditing and Continuous Monitoring
subtopics.summary: Both use automation to watch transactions often or in near real time, but they belong to different owners. Management watches its own processes to keep them in control. The audit function runs its own routines to provide independent assurance. Precise terms: continuous monitoring (a management control) and continuous auditing (an audit technique).
subtopics.key_point: Management's continuous monitoring is a control the auditor may test and then rely on. It never replaces audit evidence untested.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 490 126' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Periodic audits leave gaps between checkpoints; continuous auditing covers every transaction'><rect x='14' y='20' width='148' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='88' y='45' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Periodic</text><rect x='186' y='20' width='80' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='226' y='45' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Q1</text><rect x='290' y='20' width='80' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='330' y='45' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Q2</text><rect x='394' y='20' width='80' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='434' y='45' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Q3</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='148' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='88' y='99' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Continuous</text><rect x='186' y='74' width='288' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='330' y='99' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Every transaction, in near real time</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Periodic audits leave gaps between checkpoints. Continuous auditing looks at transactions as they occur.

subtopics.exam_tip: When continuous auditing flags an anomaly, the auditor investigates, escalates and preserves evidence. Operational actions, such as halting a process, belong to management.

subtopics.name: Making Continuous Auditing Work
subtopics.summary: Continuous auditing is only as good as the data it can reach. It needs reliable, independent access to complete source data, a design that does not slow production, and clear rules for what happens when an alert fires. Precise terms: embedded audit modules, read-only replicas and data access.
subtopics.key_point: Secure reliable, complete data access first. Deploy where risk and volume justify the cost, piloting where data is ready and then expanding by risk.
subtopics.exam_tip: A small but consistent anomaly often signals a systematic cause, so it deserves investigation even when each item is minor.

subtopics.name: Artificial Intelligence in the Audit
subtopics.summary: AI and machine learning can scan huge datasets and flag unusual items for the auditor. The auditor still decides what the flags mean and owns the conclusion. Output the auditor cannot explain or reproduce cannot support an audit opinion. Precise term: AI-assisted audit analytics, subject to the auditor's professional judgment.
subtopics.key_point: Automated output is only as reliable as the auditor's understanding of how the tool works. Accountability for the opinion stays with the human auditor.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='AI in IS audit: large datasets, AI analysis, flagged anomalies, then the auditor decides'><rect x='8' y='24' width='98' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='57' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Large datasets</text><rect x='128' y='24' width='86' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='171' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>AI analysis</text><rect x='236' y='24' width='112' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='292' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Flagged anomalies</text><rect x='370' y='24' width='102' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='421' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Auditor decides</text><line x1='108' y1='46' x2='119' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M119,42 L126,46 L119,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='216' y1='46' x2='227' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M227,42 L234,46 L227,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='350' y1='46' x2='361' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M361,42 L368,46 L361,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: AI analyzes the data and flags anomalies. The auditor investigates and makes the call.

subtopics.exam_tip: Accepting an AI tool's result as evidence without understanding or validating it is a trap.

subtopics.name: Auditing AI Systems
subtopics.summary: When the organization itself uses AI to make decisions, the auditor must check the model across its whole life: the training data, how it was built and tested, how it behaves in production, and how it is retired. Precise terms: model risk, including data bias, model drift, explainability and adversarial attacks such as prompt injection.

categories.Model: Reproducible, explainable at a risk-appropriate depth.
categories.Production: Drift monitoring, override tracking, layered controls around the model.
categories.Retirement: Preserve versions, data lineage and decision logs.

subtopics.key_point: Training-data quality is the main driver of model behavior. Watch for drift in production, use independent challenger testing for high-stakes models, and keep version and decision logs so past decisions can be reconstructed.
subtopics.exam_tip: Frozen test-set accuracy cannot reveal drift. For vendor models, combine the vendor's assurance report with testing on the organization's own data.

topics.summary: An audit only creates value when the right people understand the findings and act on them.

subtopics.name: Writing Findings and Recommendations
subtopics.summary: A strong finding says what should be happening, what is actually happening, why the gap exists, and what it could cost. Then it recommends a fix. Precise terms: criteria, condition, cause, effect (risk) and recommendation.
subtopics.key_point: The auditor recommends; management decides and implements. The auditor does not design or run the fix, because that would impair independence.
subtopics.exam_tip: Fixing the symptom is a trap. Good recommendations address the root cause.

subtopics.name: The Exit Meeting and Management Responses
subtopics.summary: Before the report is final, the auditor meets management to confirm the facts, hear context and collect action plans with owners and dates. Management may disagree. Precise terms: exit conference (closing meeting) and management response.
subtopics.key_point: Findings change only if new facts are presented. If management still disagrees, its view is reported alongside the finding, not used to remove or soften it.
subtopics.exam_tip: Delaying the report until remediation is finished is a trap. Issue on time, with management's action plans included.

subtopics.name: Report Structure, Audience, and Distribution
subtopics.summary: Different readers need different depth: the board wants the big picture, managers need the details to fix things. A layered report with an executive summary and detailed sections keeps one consistent set of conclusions for everyone. Precise terms: the audit report, its addressees and restricted distribution.
subtopics.key_point: Formal reports go to the governance body the audit function reports to, typically the audit committee, with copies to the managers responsible for fixing issues.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 494 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The reporting cycle: findings, the audit report, the management response, and auditor follow-up'><rect x='8' y='24' width='84' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='50' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Findings</text><rect x='114' y='24' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='164' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Audit report</text><rect x='236' y='24' width='136' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='304' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Management response</text><rect x='394' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='440' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Follow-up</text><line x1='94' y1='46' x2='105' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M105,42 L112,46 L105,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='216' y1='46' x2='227' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M227,42 L234,46 L227,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='374' y1='46' x2='385' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M385,42 L392,46 L385,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: The reporting cycle continues past the report: management responds, then the auditor follows up.

subtopics.exam_tip: Restricted-use sensitive findings still reach governance and responsible management. Need-to-know limits distribution; it does not hide findings from oversight.

subtopics.name: Audit Opinions
subtopics.summary: Some engagements end with a formal opinion. A clean result gets a clean opinion; significant but contained problems get a qualified one, and widespread problems an adverse one. If the auditor could not get enough evidence, no opinion is given at all. Precise terms: unqualified, qualified, adverse and disclaimer of opinion.

categories.Qualified: Significant but contained exception or limitation.
categories.Disclaimer: Unable to obtain sufficient evidence to form an opinion.

subtopics.key_point: The choice turns on how significant and how pervasive the issue is, and whether the problem is a scope limitation or an actual exception.
subtopics.exam_tip: A pervasive scope limitation with no alternative evidence leads to a disclaimer, not an adverse opinion.

subtopics.name: Escalation and Follow-Up
subtopics.summary: Some findings cannot wait for the next report: a critical issue with regulatory exposure goes to the audit committee chair promptly. After the report, the auditor checks that agreed actions were really done. Precise terms: escalation and follow-up.
subtopics.key_point: Follow-up independently verifies that management's agreed actions were implemented and effective. Its depth and timing scale with each finding's severity.
subtopics.exam_tip: Repeat findings year after year signal a remediation failure. Analyze the root cause and escalate to the audit committee for accountability.

topics.topic_name: Quality Assurance and Improvement of Audit Process
topics.summary: Auditors are audited too. A quality program checks that audit work meets standards and gets better over time.

subtopics.name: Supervision and Ongoing Monitoring
subtopics.summary: Quality starts inside each engagement. Supervisors review work papers as they are produced and check that every conclusion is backed by evidence before a report goes out. Precise terms: engagement supervision and ongoing quality monitoring.
subtopics.key_point: Ongoing monitoring is built into routine supervision of every engagement. Its value is catching substantive defects, such as unsupported conclusions, before reports are issued.
subtopics.exam_tip: Automated work-paper checkers confirm form, such as missing sign-offs. Human review is still needed for the substance of evidence and conclusions.

subtopics.name: Periodic Internal Assessments
subtopics.summary: Beyond day-to-day supervision, the function periodically reviews a sample of completed engagements. The reviewers should be auditors who did not work on those engagements. Precise term: periodic internal quality assessment, part of the quality assurance and improvement program.
subtopics.key_point: Internal assessment combines ongoing monitoring with periodic reviews by people independent of the work reviewed.
subtopics.exam_tip: An engagement-level peer review checks one audit; a program-level review checks the whole quality system. They complement each other.

subtopics.name: External Quality Assessments
subtopics.summary: Even a careful team can share blind spots. An outside assessor brings a fresh, independent view of whether the function conforms to standards. Precise term: external quality assessment, performed at least once every five years by a qualified assessor independent of the organization.
subtopics.key_point: Self-assessment alone gives the audit committee unverified assurance. A periodic independent external assessment is required.
subtopics.exam_tip: An assessor from inside the organization, even from another department, is not external.

subtopics.name: Continuous Improvement
subtopics.summary: A quality program should not only find mistakes but make the next audit better. Lessons from reviews, stakeholder feedback, repeat findings and performance measures feed back into methods, training and tools. Precise term: the improvement cycle of the quality assurance and improvement program.
subtopics.key_point: Training should close the gap between current skills and what the approved audit plan needs. Results of quality reviews are reported to the audit committee.
subtopics.exam_tip: Generic training that ignores the plan's skill needs is a weak answer. Target the specific gaps.

key_terminologies.Audit charter: The document, approved by the board or audit committee, that gives the audit function its purpose, authority, scope and reporting line.
key_terminologies.ITAF: ISACA's IT Audit Framework: mandatory standards, advisory guidelines, and example tools and techniques.
key_terminologies.Audit committee: A board committee of independent directors that oversees audit, internal control and financial reporting.
key_terminologies.Independence: Freedom, in structure and in mindset, from influences that could bias the auditor's conclusions.
key_terminologies.Self-review threat: The risk to objectivity when auditors evaluate work they themselves designed or performed.
key_terminologies.Audit universe: The complete list of everything in the organization that could be audited.
key_terminologies.Risk-based audit plan: The schedule of audits chosen and ordered by current risk.
key_terminologies.Inherent risk: The risk that exists before considering any controls.
key_terminologies.Control risk: The risk that controls fail to prevent or detect a significant problem.
key_terminologies.Detection risk: The risk that the auditor's own procedures miss a significant problem; the only part of audit risk the auditor controls.
key_terminologies.Residual risk: The risk left over after controls are applied, which management decides whether to accept.
key_terminologies.Materiality: The point at which an issue could change the decisions of those relying on the audit, considering size and nature.
key_terminologies.Reasonable assurance: A high but not absolute level of confidence, reflecting the limits of any control system.
key_terminologies.Compensating control: An alternative control that reduces the same risk when the preferred control is impractical.
key_terminologies.IT general controls: Controls over the whole IT environment, such as access, change management and operations.
key_terminologies.Compliance testing: Testing whether a control operated as designed over a period.
key_terminologies.Substantive testing: Testing transactions, balances or data directly to find misstatement.
key_terminologies.Attribute sampling: Sampling to estimate how often a control deviates.
key_terminologies.Variable sampling: Sampling to estimate a monetary amount or other quantity.
key_terminologies.Discovery sampling: Sampling designed to find at least one occurrence when fraud or critical error is suspected.
key_terminologies.Sufficient and appropriate evidence: Enough evidence (sufficient) that is relevant and reliable (appropriate) to support a conclusion.
key_terminologies.Chain of custody: A documented record of who held evidence and when, preserving its integrity for possible legal use.
key_terminologies.CAATs: Computer-assisted audit techniques: using software to test data and systems, often across full populations.
key_terminologies.Integrated test facility: A dummy entity in a live system used to compare actual processing with expected results.
key_terminologies.Continuous auditing: Automated, frequent audit testing run by the audit function for independent assurance.
key_terminologies.Continuous monitoring: Automated, ongoing oversight run by management as part of its own controls.
key_terminologies.Control self-assessment: A technique where process owners evaluate their own controls, often in a facilitated workshop.
key_terminologies.SOC 2 Type 2: A service auditor's report on a provider's controls, covering design and operating effectiveness over a period.
key_terminologies.Disclaimer of opinion: A report stating no opinion can be given because sufficient evidence could not be obtained.
key_terminologies.Follow-up: Audit work that verifies whether management implemented the agreed corrective actions.

domains.summary: This domain is about making sure IT serves the business. Governance sets direction, defines who is accountable and checks results; management plans, builds and runs IT within that direction. You will meet laws and frameworks, policies, enterprise architecture, risk management, privacy, data governance, and the day-to-day management of IT people, money, vendors, performance and quality.
domains.real_life_analogy: Think of a hospital. The board of trustees does not perform surgery, but it sets the hospital's mission, approves its budget and policies, decides how much risk is acceptable and checks that patients are safe. The medical director and department heads run daily operations within those rules, and an independent inspector reports to the trustees on whether things really work. IT governance is the trustees' role; IT management is the director's; the IS auditor is the inspector, who reports and recommends but does not run the wards.

topics.summary: Every organization operates under outside rules: laws it must obey, regulators who can inspect it, and industry standards it chooses or is contracted to follow. Governance has to know which rules apply and turn them into owned, testable controls.

subtopics.name: How Outside Rules Shape IT Governance
subtopics.summary: A hospital, a bank and an online shop all run on IT, but each answers to different rulebooks. Those rules decide what data can be kept, how long, who may see it and what must be reported. Governance cannot treat them as an IT detail; they set the boundaries strategy must stay within. The precise term is legal and regulatory compliance: conforming to the mandatory obligations that apply to the enterprise.
subtopics.example: A retailer that starts storing card data falls under the card industry's security standard through its merchant contract, even though no national law names that standard.
common_mistakes: Assuming only regulated sectors such as banks need IT governance.
Treating an industry standard as law when it is actually binding only through a contract.
subtopics.key_point: Compliance with mandatory law is non-discretionary. It is funded and treated before optional improvements, and the board stays accountable for it even when the work is delegated.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an option that treats a regulation as optional because the cost is high or the fine is small. Mandatory obligations come first when budgets are ranked.

subtopics.name: Mapping Obligations to Controls
subtopics.summary: When several regulations apply, many of them ask for the same thing, such as access reviews or logging. A smart program lists every requirement, maps it to one shared set of controls and names an owner for each. Overlapping controls are then tested once and relied on everywhere, and gaps become visible. The precise term is a compliance obligations register mapped to a unified control framework.

categories.Obligations register: A list of every law, regulation and contractual standard that applies, with its specific requirements.
categories.Control mapping: Each requirement linked to the internal control that satisfies it.
categories.Horizon scanning: Named staff watch for proposed and new rules so controls are updated before a deadline, not after a breach.

common_mistakes: Waiting for a regulator's letter before reacting to a new rule.
Letting the auditor decide which of two conflicting laws wins; that is a legal question for counsel and management.
subtopics.key_point: Map requirements to a common control set with clear owners. Test shared controls once and rely on the result; refer genuine legal conflicts to legal counsel rather than having the auditor resolve them.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: running a separate audit for each regulation. It duplicates effort and hides overlaps. Look for the answer that maps first, then tests.

subtopics.name: Industry Standards and Frameworks
subtopics.summary: Frameworks are ready-made blueprints that save an organization from inventing governance from scratch. Each answers a different question, so mature organizations combine them instead of picking one. Adopting a framework is usually voluntary, unless a regulator or contract makes it mandatory. The precise term is good-practice frameworks for the governance and management of enterprise IT.

categories.COBIT 2019: ISACA's framework for governing and managing enterprise information and technology. It separates governance (Evaluate, Direct and Monitor) from management (Align, Plan and Organize; Build, Acquire and Implement; Deliver, Service and Support; Monitor, Evaluate and Assess).
categories.ISO/IEC 38500: An international standard giving the governing body principles for overseeing the use of IT, such as conformance with laws and policies.
categories.ISO/IEC 27001: The certifiable standard for an information security management system (ISMS): scope, risk assessment, Statement of Applicability, internal audit and management review.
categories.COSO Internal Control (2013): Five linked components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring activities.
categories.ITIL 4: A service management framework built around value; its four dimensions are organizations and people, information and technology, partners and suppliers, and value streams and processes.
categories.NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: A voluntary outcome-based framework organized into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.

common_mistakes: Believing ISO 9001 or ISO/IEC 27001 certification guarantees a good product or a breach-free vendor; it certifies a management system within its scope.
Treating NIST CSF implementation tiers as maturity levels; they describe how rigorous risk governance and management practices are.
subtopics.key_point: Choose and tailor frameworks to the enterprise's goals and context. A framework is a tool for meeting objectives, not an objective in itself.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: confusing what each framework is for. COBIT is about governing and managing enterprise IT, ISO/IEC 27001 about running a security management system, ITIL about service management, and COSO about internal control.

topics.topic_name: Organizational Structure, IT Governance, and IT Strategy
topics.summary: Who decides, who does the work and who checks it. This topic separates governance from management, names the bodies that oversee IT, and shows how IT strategy is derived from business strategy.

subtopics.name: Governance Versus Management
subtopics.summary: Governance decides where the organization is going and checks that it gets there; management does the driving. The board sets direction, weighs options and watches results, while executives plan, build and run the IT that delivers. Mixing the two weakens both. The precise term is enterprise governance of information and technology (EGIT).
