subtopics.memory_aid: Board = E-D-M (Evaluate, Direct, Monitor). Management = P-B-R-M (Plan, Build, Run, Monitor).
common_mistakes: Describing the CIO's planning process as governance.
Thinking EGIT applies only to regulated industries.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Enterprise governance of IT: business strategy drives IT strategy, which delivers business value'><rect x='8' y='24' width='124' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='70' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Business strategy</text><rect x='154' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>IT strategy</text><rect x='268' y='24' width='124' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='330' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>IT delivers value</text><line x1='134' y1='46' x2='145' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M145,42 L152,46 L145,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='248' y1='46' x2='259' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M259,42 L266,46 L259,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: IT strategy is derived from business strategy, and IT earns its keep only when it delivers value the business can see.

subtopics.key_point: The board evaluates, directs and monitors; management plans, builds, runs and monitors. Accountability for governance stays with the board.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an answer where the board approves technical designs or runs projects. That is management work dressed up as oversight.

subtopics.name: Boards, Committees and Roles
subtopics.summary: Large organizations split IT oversight across several bodies, each with its own charter and decision rights. The IT strategy committee works at board level and advises on direction; the IT steering committee is a management body that ranks projects, allocates resources and tracks delivery. The audit committee oversees assurance and must be independent of management. The precise term is IT governance structure, defined through charters and decision rights.

categories.IT strategy committee: Board-level; advises the board on IT direction, emerging technology and strategic risk.
categories.IT steering committee: Senior business and IT managers; prioritizes projects, allocates resources and monitors delivery.
categories.Audit committee: Independent board members who oversee internal and external audit and the reliability of reporting.
categories.RACI chart: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. Exactly one Accountable role per outcome.

common_mistakes: Naming several Accountable roles for one outcome, so ownership falls between them.
Letting a committee review issues without the authority to escalate or enforce.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 148' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Governance structure: the board of directors holds ultimate accountability, above the CEO, the CIO and the CISO'><line x1='230' y1='48' x2='230' y2='62' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='230' y1='96' x2='230' y2='102' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='136' y1='102' x2='324' y2='102' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='136' y1='102' x2='136' y2='108' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='324' y1='102' x2='324' y2='108' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='130' y='14' width='200' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='230' y='35' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Board of Directors</text><rect x='150' y='62' width='160' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='230' y='83' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>CEO</text><rect x='56' y='108' width='160' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='136' y='129' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>CIO</text><rect x='244' y='108' width='160' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='324' y='129' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>CISO</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Accountability starts at the top: the board answers for IT governance, and executives such as the CEO, CIO and CISO carry out the direction it sets.

subtopics.key_point: Each decision belongs to one clearly chartered body with a defined escalation path. One outcome, one Accountable role.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: swapping the two committees. Project prioritization and resource allocation point to the steering committee; long-term direction advice to the board points to the strategy committee.

subtopics.name: The Three Lines Model and Audit's Place
subtopics.summary: Think of a building: the people who use it keep it safe day to day, a safety office sets rules and checks on them, and an independent inspector reports to the owners. In an organization, operational management owns and manages risk, risk and compliance functions support and challenge, and internal audit gives independent assurance to the governing body. The precise term is the IIA Three Lines Model.
common_mistakes: Treating the second line (risk, compliance) as independent assurance; only internal audit provides that.
Having audit accept a risk or choose a vendor on management's behalf.
subtopics.key_point: Management owns risk; internal audit provides independent assurance. Audit recommends and management decides, so audit must not design, run or approve the controls it will later assess.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an option that has internal audit run the risk register or sit as a voting member of the governance it audits. That creates a self-review threat to independence.

subtopics.name: IT Strategy and Strategic Planning
subtopics.summary: An IT strategy explains how technology will help the business reach its goals over the next several years. It starts from the business plan, describes a target state, and lays out a prioritized roadmap to close the gaps. Shorter tactical plans then turn that direction into this year's projects. The precise terms are the IT strategic plan and IT-business alignment.
subtopics.example: When a merger or a major breach changes the business mid-cycle, the strategy gets a focused, board-endorsed update rather than being thrown away or ignored.

categories.Strategic plan: Multi-year direction aligned to enterprise strategy.
categories.Tactical plan: Near-term initiatives, budgets and milestones that execute the strategy.
categories.IT portfolio management: Ranking and funding investments as a portfolio so the mix reflects strategy and risk.

subtopics.key_point: Alignment is proven by tracing each major IT investment to a business objective with a measure of success, not by IT efficiency numbers.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: picking the answer that measures IT activity (projects delivered, uptime) as proof of alignment. Look for the link to business outcomes.

subtopics.name: Information Security Governance
subtopics.summary: Security governance is the board making sure the organization's information is protected in line with business goals and risk appetite. It is not a separate world run only by the security team. The board stays answerable; the CISO and management do the work and report back. The precise term is information security governance, a subset of enterprise and IT governance.
common_mistakes: Approving a security policy at CISO level only; policies need top management or board authority.
Measuring awareness training by completion rates instead of behavior change.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 140' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Information security governance sits inside IT governance, which sits inside enterprise governance'><rect x='14' y='18' width='432' height='108' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='var(--accent-fill)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 3'/><text x='230' y='34' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Enterprise governance</text><rect x='58' y='46' width='344' height='72' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='var(--accent-fill)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 3'/><text x='230' y='62' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>IT governance</text><rect x='108' y='74' width='244' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='230' y='97' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Information security governance</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Security governance lives inside IT governance, which lives inside enterprise governance. It is part of the whole, not a separate silo.

subtopics.key_point: The board can delegate the execution of security to the CISO, but not the ultimate accountability. A security strategy must map to business objectives.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: 'the CISO is ultimately accountable for security.' Delegation moves the work, not the accountability.

subtopics.name: Segregation of Duties in IT
subtopics.summary: No single person should be able to start a sensitive action, approve it, carry it out and hide the evidence. Splitting those steps across people means a mistake or a fraud needs collusion to go unnoticed. When a team is too small to split duties, an independent person reviews the activity after the fact. The precise term is segregation of duties (SoD), with compensating controls where full SoD is not practical.
subtopics.example: A lone database administrator can both run changes and edit the audit log. A compensating control sends the logs to a system the administrator cannot alter, reviewed by someone outside the team.
subtopics.memory_aid: Split the four hands: request, approve, execute, record.
subtopics.key_point: SoD fails most dangerously when one person can change data or code and also alter the logs that would reveal it. Where SoD is impossible, add independent detective controls.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: accepting 'the team is small, so SoD does not apply.' The correct answer adds a compensating control such as independent log review against approved changes.

topics.topic_name: IT Policies, Standards, Procedures, and Guidelines
topics.summary: Written rules turn governance intent into daily behavior. This topic covers the four document types, how policies are created and approved, and how they stay current and are proven to work.

subtopics.name: The Four Document Types
subtopics.summary: A policy says what management wants and why, in a few stable sentences. A standard makes that intent measurable with specific mandatory requirements. A procedure gives the step-by-step actions, and a guideline offers helpful advice that people may adapt. The precise term is the policy document hierarchy, where lower documents must conform to those above.
subtopics.memory_aid: Why, What exactly, How, Hint: Policy, Standard, Procedure, Guideline.
common_mistakes: Raising an audit finding against a guideline as if it were mandatory.
Leaving a policy without a supporting standard, so implementations drift and compliance cannot be measured.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 186' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The document hierarchy: policy sets intent, standards make it mandatory and specific, procedures give step-by-step instructions, guidelines are recommended'><rect x='20' y='16' width='420' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='230' y='37' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Policy — what management intends</text><rect x='20' y='58' width='420' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='230' y='79' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Standards — mandatory specifics</text><rect x='20' y='100' width='420' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='230' y='121' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Procedures — step-by-step</text><rect x='20' y='142' width='420' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='230' y='163' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Guidelines — recommended</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Each layer gets more specific and changes more often. Only the bottom layer, guidelines, is optional.

subtopics.key_point: Policies, standards and procedures are mandatory; guidelines are advisory. A lower document that is weaker than the one above it is a compliance gap, not a valid local choice.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: a policy full of technical settings (password length, cipher names). Those specifics belong in a standard so the policy stays stable.

subtopics.name: Developing and Approving Policy
subtopics.summary: Policies can start from the top or from the ground. Top-down policies flow from business objectives and strategy, so they stay aligned with what the enterprise needs. Bottom-up policies grow out of risk assessments and day-to-day operations; they are practical but can codify local habits and miss enterprise goals. The precise terms are top-down and bottom-up policy development.
subtopics.example: A new CIO compiles teams' existing procedures into a 'policy set.' The greatest risk is that the result reflects today's habits rather than enterprise objectives.
common_mistakes: Writing policy without consulting the functions that must follow it, producing rules nobody can apply.
Letting each subsidiary write its own policy set instead of a group baseline with approved local addenda.
subtopics.key_point: Bottom-up policies come from risk assessment and operations; top-down policies come from business objectives. Either way, final approval comes from top management or the board, with input from the people who must apply them.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: approval by a functional head such as the CISO or IT manager. That gives neither enterprise authority nor business alignment.

subtopics.name: Keeping Policies Alive
subtopics.summary: A policy that is never reviewed slowly stops matching reality. Good practice reviews policies at planned intervals and whenever something significant changes, keeps one authoritative version, and assigns owners to procedures. Exceptions are allowed but controlled. The precise terms are policy review cycle, version control and the policy exception process.

categories.Review triggers: Planned intervals plus significant change: new law, reorganization, major incident, new technology.
categories.Version control: A single authoritative source so staff always follow the current rule.
categories.Exceptions: Risk-owner approval, expiry date, register, periodic review.

subtopics.key_point: An exception is accepted risk, so the risk owner approves it, it carries an expiry date, and it is tracked and reviewed. Proof that a policy works comes from testing practice, not from documents or signed acknowledgments.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: treating staff sign-offs as evidence the policy operates. Acknowledgments show awareness; only observation or testing shows operation.

topics.summary: Enterprise architecture (EA) is the city plan for an organization's processes, data, applications and technology. It keeps individual projects from building disconnected, duplicate or unsupported systems.

subtopics.name: What Enterprise Architecture Is
subtopics.summary: Without a city plan, every builder would pick their own roads and pipes. EA describes how business processes, information, applications and technology fit together and how they should evolve to support strategy. It always starts from the business layer so every system can be traced to a need. The precise term is enterprise architecture, often organized in layers such as business, data, application and technology.

categories.Data architecture: What information exists, where it lives and how it flows.
categories.Application architecture: The systems and how they interact.
categories.Technology architecture: Infrastructure, platforms and networks that host it all.

subtopics.key_point: EA exists to align IT with business strategy. Cost savings and standardization are benefits that follow, not the purpose.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: 'the main goal of EA is to cut IT costs' or 'to standardize vendors.' Choose the alignment answer.

subtopics.name: Current State, Target State and the Roadmap
subtopics.summary: You cannot plan a journey without knowing where you are. EA documents the current architecture, describes the desired target, analyzes the gaps, and sequences the work into a transition roadmap. That roadmap then guides which projects get approved. The precise terms are baseline (as-is) architecture, target (to-be) architecture and gap analysis.
subtopics.example: After a merger, overlapping systems are rationalized by mapping each required business capability to the platforms that serve it; cost is one input, not the deciding one.
subtopics.key_point: Document the current-state baseline before planning the move to the target. A target with no gap analysis and roadmap changes nothing.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: jumping straight to designing the target architecture. Without the baseline, gaps and migration effort cannot be measured.

subtopics.name: Governing and Auditing Architecture
subtopics.summary: Architecture only matters if projects follow it. An architecture review board checks designs and purchases, and any approved deviation is logged as a waiver with an owner and a sunset date. A rising waiver rate is a signal that the standards themselves are out of date. The precise terms are architecture governance, architecture review board (ARB) and waiver register.
subtopics.example: Auditors use EA data-flow and interface views to find control points where data enters, moves and changes between systems.
common_mistakes: Treating waivers as permanent rather than as technical debt with a remediation date.
Never revisiting standards, so teams route around them.
subtopics.key_point: EA effectiveness is shown by projects conforming to standards and by tracked, time-bound waivers, not by attractive models or executive endorsements.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: business units buying technology directly to save time. Bypassing architecture review creates duplicate data stores, unmanaged integrations and long-term support and security risk.

topics.summary: ERM is how the whole organization decides which risks to take, which to reduce and who answers for each. IT risk is one part of that picture, managed against the appetite the board sets.

subtopics.name: Building a Risk Management Program
subtopics.summary: A risk program is a repeating cycle, not a one-time project. Risks are identified, assessed, given a response, and monitored, and the loop runs again as the business and threats change. It rests on governance: a board-approved appetite, named risk owners and an accountable internal lead. The precise term is the risk management life cycle within an ERM program.

categories.Risk register: The working record of each risk, its owner, rating, chosen response and status, with an audit trail of decisions.
categories.Inherent risk: Exposure before any controls are applied.
categories.Residual risk: Exposure left after controls; it must sit within appetite or be formally accepted.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 412 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Risk management program: identify, assess, respond, monitor'><rect x='8' y='24' width='84' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='50' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Identify</text><rect x='114' y='24' width='78' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='153' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Assess</text><rect x='214' y='24' width='84' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='256' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Respond</text><rect x='320' y='24' width='84' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='362' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Monitor</text><line x1='94' y1='46' x2='105' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M105,42 L112,46 L105,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='194' y1='46' x2='205' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M205,42 L212,46 L205,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='300' y1='46' x2='311' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M311,42 L318,46 L311,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: The core cycle: find the risk, size it, decide what to do, then keep watching. The loop repeats because risk keeps moving.

subtopics.key_point: A register full of rated risks with no responses or monitoring gives false assurance. Expertise can be bought in, but accountability for the program cannot be outsourced.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: judging maturity by the existence of tools, staff or a register. A mature program shows in behavior: risk information changes business decisions.

subtopics.name: Risk Appetite, Tolerance and Ownership
subtopics.summary: Before deciding what to do about a risk, you need to know how much risk the organization is willing to carry. Appetite is the board's broad stance on risk in pursuit of its goals. Tolerance turns that stance into a specific, measurable limit for a given risk, and capacity is the most loss the organization could absorb. The precise terms are risk appetite, risk tolerance and risk capacity.
subtopics.example: A CIO wants to accept excess dependence on one cloud provider to keep a discount. That exceeds appetite, so the decision belongs to senior management, documented, not to the CIO.
common_mistakes: Letting the IT manager approve exceptions that accept enterprise risk.
Waiting for the annual cycle to register a serious new risk; it is assessed and treated when it appears.
subtopics.key_point: Risk above appetite is escalated to senior management to treat or formally accept. Operational owners and auditors cannot accept it on the organization's behalf.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: confusing appetite with tolerance. 'We accept moderate risk to grow' is appetite; 'no more than four hours of outage a year' is tolerance.

subtopics.name: Risk Analysis Methods
subtopics.summary: Risk can be sized with words, with scored scales, or with money. Qualitative analysis uses ratings like high, medium and low; semi-quantitative analysis uses calibrated numeric scales; quantitative analysis estimates likely loss in currency. The right method depends on how good the data is and what decision the result must support. The precise terms are qualitative, semi-quantitative and quantitative risk analysis.

categories.SLE (single loss expectancy): Expected loss from one occurrence: asset value multiplied by exposure factor.
categories.ARO (annualized rate of occurrence): How many times per year the event is expected.
categories.ALE (annualized loss expectancy): SLE multiplied by ARO: the expected loss per year.
categories.FAIR: A quantitative model that splits risk into loss event frequency and loss magnitude, estimates each as a range, and simulates a distribution of annual loss.

subtopics.memory_aid: ALE = SLE × ARO. One loss times how often per year equals the yearly loss.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Qualitative risk analysis uses descriptive ratings; quantitative uses numeric values'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Qualitative</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Ratings: high, medium, low</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Quantitative</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Numbers: ALE = SLE × ARO</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Qualitative analysis describes risk in ratings; quantitative analysis puts a money value on it, which needs more and better data.

subtopics.key_point: Pick the method that fits the available data and the decision. Quantitative is more precise only when the inputs are reliable.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: assuming quantitative is always 'best.' With poor data, false precision misleads decision makers.

subtopics.name: Choosing a Risk Response
subtopics.summary: Once a risk is understood, management has four basic choices. It can accept the risk, reduce it with controls, transfer part of the financial impact to someone else, or avoid it by changing or stopping the activity. Whatever remains after the choice is residual risk, which must fit within appetite. The precise term is risk treatment (also called risk response).
common_mistakes: Accepting a high-likelihood, high-impact risk with no fix just because treatment is expensive.
Ranking risks by impact alone and ignoring likelihood.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The four risk responses: accept, avoid, transfer, reduce'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Accept — within appetite</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Avoid — drop the activity</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Transfer — insure or contract</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Reduce — add controls</text></svg>
illustration.caption: The four responses. Reduce is also called mitigate. Whatever is left after the choice is residual risk.

subtopics.key_point: When no control or insurance can bring a risk within appetite, avoid it. Under budget limits, treat mandatory obligations first, then rank by expected loss, and escalate the rest for formal acceptance.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: 'transfer the risk by outsourcing.' Insurance or contracts can shift financial impact, but accountability for the outcome stays with the organization.

topics.summary: Privacy is about the fair and lawful use of information about people. Security protects the data; privacy decides whether it should be collected and used at all, for what purpose and for how long.

subtopics.name: Foundations of a Privacy Program
subtopics.summary: A privacy program starts by knowing what personal data the organization has, why it has it and on what legal basis. An accountable owner, clear policies and staff who know their part come next; security controls support the program but are not the program. Common principles include using data only for stated purposes, collecting no more than needed, and keeping it no longer than needed. The precise terms are accountability, purpose limitation, data minimization and storage limitation.

categories.Lawful basis: The legal ground for processing, such as consent, contract, legal obligation or legitimate interests.
categories.Privacy stewards: Named people in each business unit who build privacy steps into normal processes.
categories.Global baseline: One set of common requirements across jurisdictions, with a mapped layer for local differences.

common_mistakes: Treating privacy as the same thing as security.
Relying on contract necessity for marketing personalization; it usually needs consent or a documented legitimate-interests assessment.
subtopics.key_point: Privacy starts with accountable governance and an inventory of personal data, purposes and lawful bases. Encryption alone does not make processing lawful.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an answer that starts the privacy program by buying a security tool. Governance and the data inventory come first.

subtopics.name: Privacy Documentation and Impact Assessments
subtopics.summary: Privacy needs paperwork that serves different readers. The internal privacy policy tells staff how the organization handles personal data; the external privacy notice tells individuals what happens to theirs. Regulators can ask for a record of processing activities, and risky new processing needs an impact assessment before it starts. The precise terms are privacy policy, privacy notice, record of processing activities (RoPA) and data protection impact assessment (DPIA).

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 108' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='A privacy policy is the internal rulebook; a privacy notice is what individuals are told'><rect x='14' y='28' width='206' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='117' y='54' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Privacy policy</text><rect x='246' y='28' width='200' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='346' y='54' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Privacy notice</text><text x='117' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>internal — how the org handles data</text><text x='346' y='92' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>external — what individuals are told</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Two documents with two audiences: the policy guides the organization's own people, the notice informs the individuals whose data is used.

subtopics.key_point: A DPIA is done before high-risk processing begins, to test necessity, proportionality and risks to individuals.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: running the DPIA after go-live. By then the design choices it should have shaped are already fixed.

subtopics.name: Privacy by Design and by Default
subtopics.summary: Privacy works best when it is built in from the start, like wiring planned before the walls go up. By design means privacy requirements and checks appear from the requirements stage through testing. By default means the out-of-the-box setting collects and shares only what is needed, and anything more intrusive must be switched on deliberately for a defined purpose. The precise terms are data protection by design and data protection by default.
subtopics.key_point: Build privacy in from requirements onward with checks at each stage; do not inspect it in at the end.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: confusing the two. 'Least data collected unless the user opts in' is by default; 'privacy requirements in every SDLC phase' is by design.

subtopics.name: Individual Rights and Cross-Border Transfers
subtopics.summary: People can ask what data an organization holds about them, ask to correct it or to have it erased, among other rights. The organization must confirm the requester really is that person and answer within the legal deadline. Sending personal data to another country also needs a valid transfer mechanism and, often, an assessment of the destination's risks. The precise terms are data subject rights and transborder data flow.

categories.Transfer mechanisms: Adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses and similar safeguards, backed by a documented transfer impact assessment where required.
categories.Audit approach: Test actual data flows against the documented mechanisms; documents alone do not prove where data goes.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 448 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Handling a data subject request: receive it, verify the requester identity, respond by the legal deadline'><rect x='8' y='24' width='118' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='67' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Request received</text><rect x='148' y='24' width='112' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='204' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Verify identity</text><rect x='282' y='24' width='158' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='361' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Respond by the deadline</text><line x1='128' y1='46' x2='139' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M139,42 L146,46 L139,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='262' y1='46' x2='273' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M273,42 L280,46 L273,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: A rights request in three steps: log it, confirm the requester's identity, and answer within the legal time limit.

subtopics.key_point: When two privacy laws apply to one request, meet both sets of obligations and the shorter deadline. Erasure has limits: data a law requires you to keep is retained, restricted and erased later.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: releasing data to a requester without verifying identity. That turns a rights request into a breach.

topics.summary: Data governance answers who owns each kind of data, where it is, how sensitive it is and how long it is kept. Classification is the foundation that tells every other control how hard to protect what.

subtopics.name: Data Ownership and Custodianship
subtopics.summary: Every important data set needs a business person who answers for it. That owner decides how sensitive it is, who may access it and how it may be used. IT teams or cloud providers that store and process the data act as custodians, following the owner's rules. The precise terms are data owner, data custodian and data steward.

categories.Data owner: Senior business role accountable for classification, access and use.
categories.Data custodian: Stores, protects and processes data according to the owner's rules (IT, a provider).
categories.Data steward: Maintains data quality, definitions and inventory entries day to day.

subtopics.key_point: Ownership follows business accountability. Moving data to a vendor or the cloud does not move ownership; the provider becomes a custodian under contract.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: naming IT or the cloud provider as the data owner because they hold the data. Holding is custody, not ownership.

subtopics.name: Data Inventory
subtopics.summary: You cannot protect data you do not know you have. A data inventory lists data assets, where they live, who owns them and what they contain. It stays accurate only when adding new data is part of normal change processes and when discovery scans are regularly reconciled against it. The precise term is data inventory (sometimes data catalog or data map).
subtopics.key_point: Keep the inventory current through stewards and change processes, and catch drift with independent, recurring reconciliation against discovery results.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: a one-time inventory project. It is out of date as soon as the next system goes live.

subtopics.name: Data Classification
subtopics.summary: Classification sorts data by how much harm would follow if it were disclosed, altered or lost. Each level comes with handling rules, such as who may see it, whether it must be encrypted, and how it is disposed of. A few clear levels work better than many fine ones. The precise term is a data classification scheme.
common_mistakes: Letting IT classify business data on the owner's behalf.
Deploying data loss prevention before data is classified, so policies cannot tell sensitive from routine.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 186' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Data classification levels from public, least sensitive, up to restricted, most sensitive'><rect x='20' y='16' width='420' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='230' y='37' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Public — no harm if disclosed</text><rect x='20' y='58' width='420' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='230' y='79' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Internal use only</text><rect x='20' y='100' width='420' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='230' y='121' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Confidential</text><rect x='20' y='142' width='420' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='230' y='163' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Restricted — highest protection</text></svg>
illustration.caption: An example scheme. Labels and number of levels vary by organization; what matters is that each level carries its own handling rules.

subtopics.key_point: Classification comes first: it drives proportionate protection, data loss prevention rules and retention. The owner assigns the level.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: too many levels or levels with no handling rules attached. Labels that do not change behavior are decoration.

subtopics.name: Retention and Disposal
subtopics.summary: Data should be kept as long as the law and the business need it, and then securely destroyed. Keeping it too briefly breaks legal duties; keeping it too long adds breach exposure and can break privacy law. Each category of data gets its own retention period with a documented reason. The precise terms are records retention schedule and secure disposal.
subtopics.key_point: Set retention per data category with a documented basis, meeting each law's minimum without keeping personal data longer than needed.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: 'keep everything forever to be safe.' Over-retention is itself a compliance and breach risk.

topics.summary: IT runs on people, money, capacity and the organization's ability to change. This topic covers how those resources are planned, funded and controlled so they serve strategy.

subtopics.name: Managing IT People
subtopics.summary: People are both IT's greatest asset and a source of risk. Controls follow the employee's journey: screening and agreements when they join, training and role-based access while they work, and prompt removal of access when they leave. Mandatory vacations and job rotation help reveal fraud, because someone else steps into the role. The precise term is IT human resource management.

categories.Joining: Background checks, confidentiality agreements, least-privilege access.
categories.During employment: Training, mandatory vacation, job rotation, access reviews, succession planning.
categories.Leaving: Same-day access removal, return of assets, knowledge transfer.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 364 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='HR security controls across the employee lifecycle: joining, during employment, leaving'><rect x='8' y='24' width='90' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='53' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Joining</text><rect x='120' y='24' width='124' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='182' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>During employment</text><rect x='266' y='24' width='90' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='311' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Leaving</text><line x1='100' y1='46' x2='111' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M111,42 L118,46 L111,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='246' y1='46' x2='257' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M257,42 L264,46 L257,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: People controls across the employee journey. The leaving stage is where access is most often left behind.

subtopics.key_point: Mandatory leave and cross-training expose concealed fraud; a privileged user who avoids both is a red flag. Competence comes from role-based skills frameworks and periodic reassessment.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: treating leaver access removal as an HR paperwork task. Delayed revocation is one of the most common real control failures.

subtopics.name: IT Financial Management and Investment
subtopics.summary: IT money should go where it creates the most business value at an acceptable risk. Business cases quantify expected benefits and define how success will be measured; portfolio management ranks investments as a set and rebalances them when circumstances change. Chargeback and cloud cost practices make business units see and own what they consume. The precise terms are IT portfolio management, business case, chargeback and FinOps.

categories.Business case: Costs, quantified benefits, risks and success measures for one investment.
categories.Chargeback: Transparent allocation of IT cost to consumers, traceable to actual cost and driven by their usage.
categories.FinOps: Cloud cost discipline: tag spend, allocate it, and make consuming teams accountable for it.

subtopics.key_point: Value is shown by business outcomes realized from IT investment, not by money spent or projects delivered. Material portfolio changes go back to the body that approved the portfolio.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: cutting IT cost evenly across all areas. Cuts should follow risk and value, protecting regulatory and critical services and documenting risks accepted.

subtopics.name: Capacity and Resource Planning
subtopics.summary: Running out of capacity hurts the business just as much as an outage. Planning starts from validated business demand forecasts, sets headroom thresholds, and accounts for how long it takes to buy or provision more. When teams compete for the same resource, a governance forum with clear decision rights settles it. The precise term is capacity and resource planning.
subtopics.key_point: Start from business demand, not from last year's usage alone, and decide contested resources through an accountable forum.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: fixing disputes by giving the resource to whoever escalates loudest. The answer defines decision rights.

subtopics.name: Enterprise Change Management
subtopics.summary: New systems deliver value only when people actually work differently. Enterprise change management is the people side of change: understanding stakeholders, communicating, training and reinforcing new habits. It differs from IT change management, which controls technical changes to production. The precise term is organizational (enterprise) change management.

categories.IT change management: Requests, testing, approval and release of technical changes to production.
categories.Enterprise change management: Stakeholder analysis, communication, training, feedback and reinforcement for people.

common_mistakes: Running a merger integration on IT deadlines instead of business go/no-go criteria.
One-way announcements with no channel for stakeholder feedback.
subtopics.key_point: Major initiatives need both IT change management and enterprise change management. Honest status reporting to governance matters most, because misleading reports disable course correction.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: assuming the technical change process covers adoption. A system can pass every release gate and still fail because staff never changed how they work.

topics.summary: Much of IT is now delivered by outside providers. Vendor management covers deciding what to source, choosing and contracting carefully, watching performance and risk, and leaving cleanly. Throughout, accountability stays with the customer.

subtopics.name: Sourcing Decisions
subtopics.summary: Before outsourcing, an organization asks what it should keep doing itself. Functions that are strategic, differentiating or knowledge-intensive, or where losing control would be unacceptable, are strong candidates to stay in-house. Where outsourced work is delivered from also matters: onshore, near-shore or offshore trade cost against collaboration and oversight. The precise term is sourcing strategy.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 114' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Work can be outsourced to a vendor under an SLA and right-to-audit, but accountability for the data stays with your organization'><rect x='14' y='30' width='170' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='99' y='56' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Your organization</text><text x='233' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>SLA, right to audit</text><line x1='190' y1='52' x2='271' y2='52' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M271,48 L278,52 L271,56 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='282' y='30' width='164' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='364' y='56' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Vendor does the work</text><text x='230' y='98' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Accountability for the data stays with your organization</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Outsourcing moves the work to a vendor under contract. Accountability for the data and the result stays home.

subtopics.key_point: Outsourcing transfers the work, never the accountability. The auditor checks that management weighed all material risks beyond cost, but does not make the decision.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: choosing purely on price. Cost advantages shift over time, while lost capability is hard to rebuild.

subtopics.name: Due Diligence, Contracts and SLAs
subtopics.summary: Checking a vendor before signing should be as deep as the risk it brings. Vendors are tiered by the sensitivity of data they handle, how critical the service is and regulatory impact. The contract then protects the customer: measurable service levels with consequences, a right to audit, security and data clauses, and an exit plan agreed while leverage is highest. The precise terms are vendor due diligence, risk tiering and service level agreement (SLA).

categories.Right to audit: Lets the customer or its auditors examine the vendor's controls.
categories.Exit provisions: Data return, verified deletion, transition assistance and knowledge transfer.
categories.Service credits: Financial remedies when service levels are missed.

subtopics.key_point: An SLA protects the customer only when targets are measurable and backed by consequences such as service credits and exit rights. Negotiate the exit strategy before signing.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: accepting one certificate or questionnaire as full due diligence for a critical provider.

subtopics.name: Monitoring, Assurance and Offboarding
subtopics.summary: Signing the contract is the start, not the finish. The customer measures service levels itself, watches for changes in the vendor's risk, and reviews independent assurance reports. Repeated incidents should trigger a fresh look at the whole relationship. When the relationship ends, offboarding keeps service running and confirms data is returned and deleted. The precise terms are third-party monitoring, SOC reports and vendor offboarding.

categories.SOC 1: Controls relevant to customers' financial reporting.
categories.SOC 2 Type 1: Design of controls over security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy at a point in time.
categories.SOC 2 Type 2: Design and operating effectiveness of those controls over a period, with test results.
categories.SOC 3: A short general-use report on the same criteria, without test details.

subtopics.key_point: Verify vendor performance with customer-side measurement and independent signals rather than vendor self-reporting. After a vendor breach, the customer starts its own response and assesses its own notification duties.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: requesting a SOC 3 report to rely on controls. A SOC 2 Type 2 report includes tests and results over a period; SOC 3 is a general-use summary.

subtopics.name: Cloud Governance
subtopics.summary: Cloud services split security duties between the customer and the provider, and the split moves with the service model. With infrastructure services the customer manages much of the stack; with software services the provider manages most of it. In every model the customer still owns its data, identities and configuration choices. The precise terms are the shared responsibility model and IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

illustration.caption: Moving from IaaS to SaaS, the provider manages more of the stack. The customer's share shrinks but never disappears.

subtopics.key_point: The customer keeps accountability for its data and must continuously evidence that its own configurations stay within an approved baseline. Multi-cloud needs one consistent control layer across providers.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: 'the provider is responsible for security in SaaS.' The provider runs more of the stack, but data, access and use stay with the customer.

topics.summary: What gets measured gets managed, but only if the right things are measured honestly. This topic covers the three kinds of indicator, how to design reliable metrics and how to report them to governance.

subtopics.name: KPIs, KRIs and KCIs
subtopics.summary: Three kinds of gauge answer three questions. Are we reaching our goal? Is a risk getting worse? Is a control working? Mixing them up leads to the wrong action. The precise terms are key performance indicator (KPI), key risk indicator (KRI) and key control indicator (KCI).
subtopics.example: Days since the last patch cycle trending up is a KRI. Percentage of changes with documented approval is a KCI. Percentage of online orders completed without error is a KPI.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 470 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='KPIs measure performance, KRIs warn of rising risk, KCIs measure control effectiveness'><rect x='14' y='24' width='140' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='84' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>KPI</text><rect x='166' y='24' width='140' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='236' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>KRI</text><rect x='318' y='24' width='140' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='388' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>KCI</text><text x='84' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>how well we perform</text><text x='236' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>risk rising — early warning</text><text x='388' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>is the control working</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Three different questions: how well are we doing, is risk rising, and is the control doing its job.

subtopics.key_point: A KPI measures goal achievement, a KRI is a leading signal of rising exposure for a specific risk, and a KCI shows whether a control operates as designed. KRI thresholds need owners and escalation paths.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: picking a KPI when the stem asks for an early warning. 'Before the event happens' points to a KRI.

subtopics.name: Designing Metrics That Tell the Truth
subtopics.summary: A metric can look green while the strategy fails. Good metrics come from the critical success factors of an objective, use one agreed definition and calculation, start from a measured baseline, and have targets approved by someone other than the team being measured. The precise terms are critical success factor (CSF), baseline and target-setting integrity.
common_mistakes: Comparing units that calculate the same metric differently.
Benchmarking against peers whose scope and service levels differ.
subtopics.key_point: Derive KPIs from critical success factors, and never lower a target just to stay green. Data should come from systems of record with independent validation.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an activity count, such as tickets closed, offered as proof of an outcome. Activity can rise while results get worse.

subtopics.name: Reporting to Governance
subtopics.summary: Boards need a short view at their altitude: goals, targets, trends and exceptions. The IT balanced scorecard is one way to keep that view balanced across financial, customer or user, internal process, and learning and growth perspectives. Capability or maturity assessments show how well processes are managed, which guides improvement. The precise terms are performance reporting, IT balanced scorecard and capability assessment.

categories.Customer or user: Satisfaction and service to the business.
categories.Internal process: Efficiency and quality of IT processes.
categories.Learning and growth: Skills, innovation and readiness for the future.

subtopics.key_point: Board reporting is concise, outcome-focused and linked to enterprise goals. Before relying on a management report, the auditor tests its data back to source records.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: sending the board detailed operational statistics. Governance needs exceptions and trends against goals, not raw volume.

topics.topic_name: Quality Assurance and Quality Management of IT
topics.summary: Quality means IT products and services are fit for the business purpose they serve. Quality management builds that in through standards, independent assurance and continual improvement.

subtopics.name: Quality Assurance Versus Quality Control
subtopics.summary: A bakery can check every loaf at the end, or it can control the recipe, ingredients and oven at every step. Checking finished products catches defects late; building quality into each step prevents them. Both have a place, but prevention is cheaper. The precise terms are quality control (QC, inspecting outputs) and quality assurance (QA, assuring the process).
subtopics.memory_aid: Assurance = process, before. Control = product, after.
subtopics.key_point: QA prevents defects by building quality into each process stage; QC detects defects in finished products. Faster end-of-line testing is still QC.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: 'automate the final tests' offered as a way to strengthen quality assurance. It speeds inspection but defects are still found late.

subtopics.name: Quality Management Systems and Methods
subtopics.summary: A quality management system is the organization's documented way of achieving quality: standards, roles, reviews and measurements. Several methods help, and they complement each other. Certification proves the system exists and is followed within its scope, not that every product is good. The precise term is quality management system (QMS).

categories.ISO 9001: Certifiable international standard for a quality management system.
categories.Six Sigma: Statistical method for reducing variation and defects in high-volume processes.
categories.COBIT APO11 (Managed Quality): Builds quality into IT processes through standards, assurance, measurement and improvement.
categories.Cost of quality: Splits spending into prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure to show where investment lowers total cost.

subtopics.key_point: Quality criteria must trace to business and user requirements, and reviews need documented standards to judge against. Match the improvement method to the problem.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: treating a vendor's ISO 9001 certificate as a guarantee of product quality. It certifies the management system.

subtopics.name: Independence and Continual Improvement
subtopics.summary: A reviewer who reports to the team being reviewed cannot say no easily. QA works best when it is organizationally independent and can reject a release without pressure. When the same defects keep returning, the fix is to find the root cause and correct the process. The precise terms are QA independence, root cause analysis and continual improvement.
subtopics.example: For outsourced development, quality criteria go into the contract and are checked at staged acceptance reviews instead of being assumed.
subtopics.key_point: QA must be independent of the work it reviews. Recurring defects call for root cause analysis and process correction.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: fixing each recurring defect one at a time. The answer that changes the process that produces them is stronger.

key_terminologies.EGIT: Enterprise governance of information and technology: the board's direction and oversight so IT supports strategy and creates value.
key_terminologies.COBIT 2019: ISACA's framework for governing and managing enterprise IT, separating governance objectives from management objectives.
key_terminologies.EDM: Evaluate, Direct and Monitor, the governance activities performed by the board.
key_terminologies.IT steering committee: A management-level body that prioritizes IT projects, allocates resources and monitors delivery.
key_terminologies.IT strategy committee: A board-level body that advises the board on IT direction and strategic technology risk.
key_terminologies.Three Lines Model: The IIA model in which management owns risk, risk and compliance functions support and challenge, and internal audit provides independent assurance.
key_terminologies.RACI: A responsibility chart naming who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed, with one Accountable role per outcome.
key_terminologies.Segregation of duties (SoD): Dividing a sensitive process so no one person can initiate, approve, execute and conceal it.
key_terminologies.Compensating control: An alternative control, often detective, used when a preferred control such as full SoD is not practical.
key_terminologies.Policy: A short, stable, mandatory statement of management intent, approved at the top of the organization.
key_terminologies.Standard: A mandatory, specific requirement that makes a policy measurable.
key_terminologies.Guideline: Advisory good practice that people may adapt; not mandatory.
key_terminologies.Enterprise architecture (EA): A structured description of how business, data, applications and technology fit together and should evolve.
key_terminologies.Architecture waiver: An approved, time-bound deviation from architecture standards, treated as technical debt.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: The broad amount and type of risk the board is willing to pursue to meet its objectives.
key_terminologies.Risk tolerance: A specific, measurable limit on variation for a particular risk, derived from appetite.
key_terminologies.Residual risk: The risk that remains after controls and other treatments are applied.
key_terminologies.ALE: Annualized loss expectancy: single loss expectancy multiplied by the annualized rate of occurrence.
key_terminologies.FAIR: A quantitative risk model that estimates loss event frequency and loss magnitude as ranges and simulates annual loss.
key_terminologies.Risk treatment: The chosen response to a risk: accept, reduce, transfer or avoid.
key_terminologies.DPIA: Data protection impact assessment, done before high-risk processing of personal data begins.
key_terminologies.RoPA: Record of processing activities: a register of what personal data is processed, why, with whom and for how long.
key_terminologies.Privacy by default: Settings that, out of the box, process only the personal data needed for the stated purpose.
key_terminologies.Data owner: The business role accountable for a data set's classification, access and use.
key_terminologies.Data custodian: The party that stores and processes data according to the owner's rules, such as IT or a cloud provider.
key_terminologies.Data classification: Grouping data by the harm its exposure or misuse would cause, with handling rules for each level.
key_terminologies.SLA: Service level agreement: measurable service targets with consequences when they are missed.
key_terminologies.SOC 2 Type 2: An independent report on the design and operating effectiveness of a service organization's controls over a period, with test results.
key_terminologies.Shared responsibility model: The split of security duties between cloud customer and provider, which varies by service model.
key_terminologies.KPI / KRI / KCI: Indicators of goal achievement, rising risk exposure, and control effectiveness, respectively.

domains.domain_name: Information Systems Acquisition, Development and Implementation
domains.summary: This domain follows a system from idea to everyday use. Part A covers deciding whether a system is worth it, running the project, choosing how to build or buy it, and designing controls in from the start. Part B covers testing, controlled release, moving data and users across, and checking afterward that the promised benefits arrived. Throughout, the IS auditor gives independent advice and assurance while management makes the decisions.
domains.real_life_analogy: Think of renovating and moving into a new home. First you decide whether it is worth the money and compare options, including staying put (business case). You agree plans and a budget with a contractor, and any extra work needs a signed change order (project governance and change control). Before moving in you do a walk-through and fix anything serious (readiness testing). Movers count boxes when packing and again when unloading (data conversion reconciliation). A few months later you check whether the bills and comfort match what you were promised (post-implementation review). The IS auditor is like an independent home inspector: they check and report, but you, the owner, make the decisions.

subtopics.name: Who Does What on a Project
subtopics.summary: Every project needs someone who wants it, someone who runs it, and a group that steers it. The sponsor is the senior business leader who pays for the project and answers for its benefits. The project manager plans and delivers the work, and the steering committee makes the calls that are too big for the project manager. Precise terms: project sponsor, project manager, steering committee, project management office (PMO).

categories.Project sponsor: Senior business owner. Funds the project, approves the business case and is accountable for realizing the benefits.
categories.Project manager: Runs the project day to day: plans, schedules, coordinates people and manages scope, time and cost within delegated limits.
categories.Steering committee: Senior decision makers from the business and IT. Its members must have authority to commit resources and resolve issues, or it cannot govern.
categories.Project management office (PMO): Sets standards and methods, supports project managers and consolidates reporting. It enables delivery; it does not decide funding or priorities.
categories.IS auditor: Gives independent advice and reviews at key points. Does not design, build or approve the system, because that would mean auditing its own work.

subtopics.key_point: Accountability sits with the business: the sponsor owns the business case and the benefits, and the IS auditor stays independent, advising and reviewing but never running the project.
common_mistakes: Treating the steering committee as a status-update audience. It exists to make decisions, so it needs members who can commit money and people.
Thinking the PMO approves funding. It supports and reports; portfolio governance decides what gets funded.
subtopics.exam_tip: When a stem asks who should approve, fund or own benefits, look for the sponsor or steering committee. An answer that gives the decision to the auditor or the PMO is the trap.

subtopics.name: Charter, Scope and Project Structure
subtopics.summary: Before work starts, a short document makes the project official and says who is in charge. After that, the agreed scope is the line in the sand: anything new must go through a formal change request, not a hallway conversation. How much power the project manager has also depends on how the organization is structured. Precise terms: project charter, scope baseline, scope creep, change control.

categories.Functional structure: Staff stay in their departments and report to line managers; the project manager has little authority.
categories.Matrix structure: Staff report to both a line manager and the project manager; authority is shared.
categories.Projectized structure: The team reports to the project manager, who has full authority over project resources.

subtopics.key_point: The charter, approved by the sponsor, formally authorizes the project and gives the project manager authority over resources. Scope changes are decided by management through change control and rebaselining.
common_mistakes: Confusing the work breakdown structure with authorization. The WBS breaks down deliverables after the project is approved.
Absorbing small scope additions informally. Each one should go through change control so its cost, time and risk impact is decided by management.
subtopics.exam_tip: Two traps: picking the business case when asked what authorizes the project (the business case justifies; the charter authorizes), and accepting "just add it in" scope growth without impact analysis.

subtopics.name: Scheduling and the Critical Path
subtopics.summary: A project is a web of tasks, and some must wait for others to finish. If you trace every chain of dependent tasks from start to finish, the longest chain sets the earliest possible end date. Any delay on that chain delays the whole project, while other tasks have some spare time. Precise terms: critical path method (CPM), slack or float, PERT, Gantt chart.

categories.Gantt chart: A bar chart of tasks against a calendar. Good for showing timing and progress.
categories.PERT: Estimates task time from optimistic, most likely and pessimistic guesses, to handle uncertainty.
categories.Critical path method: Finds the longest chain of dependent tasks, which fixes the shortest possible project duration.
categories.Timebox: A fixed period with a fixed end date; scope flexes to fit the time instead of the other way around.
