illustration.caption: Only the longest chain of dependent tasks decides when the project finishes. Shorter chains have slack and can absorb some delay.

subtopics.key_point: Protect the critical path. Its tasks have zero slack, so that is where schedule risk and extra resources should be focused.
common_mistakes: Counting tasks instead of adding up durations when finding the critical path.
Assuming every late task makes the project late.
subtopics.exam_tip: The critical path is the longest path in time, not the path with the most tasks. Also, a delay on a non-critical task does not move the end date unless it uses up all its slack.

subtopics.name: Estimating, Tracking Cost and Escalating Risk
subtopics.summary: Good estimates start with a fair measure of how big the software is, and good tracking compares what was spent with what was achieved. When the numbers drift badly, or a risk grows beyond what the project manager may accept, it goes up the chain. Spare money held back for surprises is not the project manager's to spend freely. Precise terms: function point analysis, earned value management (EVM), cost performance index (CPI), schedule performance index (SPI), management reserve.

categories.Function point analysis: Sizes software by the functions it delivers (inputs, outputs, files, inquiries, interfaces). It does not depend on the programming language, so it works for early estimates.
categories.Lines of code: Sizes by code written. Depends on language and style, and is only known late.
categories.CPI: Earned value divided by actual cost. Below 1.0 means you are getting less work per dollar than planned.
categories.SPI: Earned value divided by planned value. Below 1.0 means less work done than scheduled.
categories.Contingency reserve vs management reserv: Contingency covers known risks and is inside the baseline. Management reserve covers unknowns, sits outside the baseline and needs sponsor approval to use.

subtopics.key_point: Variances well below plan rarely fix themselves and need corrective action. The management reserve sits outside the cost baseline, so every drawdown needs sponsor or steering committee approval, with the reason recorded.
common_mistakes: Trusting lines of code to compare productivity across different languages.
Keeping a risk at project level after it exceeds the project manager's delegated tolerance instead of escalating it.
subtopics.exam_tip: A CPI or SPI below 1.0 means over budget or behind schedule; above 1.0 is good. Watch for answers that let the project manager quietly use the management reserve, or that wait for a mid-project variance to "even out".

subtopics.name: Closing a Project and Lessons Learned
subtopics.summary: A project does not end when the code ships; it ends when the business formally accepts the result. Closing means releasing people and budget, finishing the financial paperwork, archiving project records and writing down what went well and what did not. Those lessons only matter if the next project can find and use them. Precise terms: formal acceptance, project closure, lessons learned.
subtopics.key_point: Closure follows formal acceptance, and lessons learned add value only when they are stored where future projects can find and apply them.
common_mistakes: Closing the project before the business owner has signed off acceptance.
Treating lessons learned as a blame exercise instead of a reusable record.
subtopics.exam_tip: A lessons-learned document filed away and never read is a common distractor. The better answer makes the lessons searchable and part of how the next project is planned.

subtopics.name: Building a Sound Business Case
subtopics.summary: A business case is the argument for spending the money. It should compare real options, including doing nothing, and say exactly what benefits are expected, how they will be measured and who will deliver them. It is not a one-time document: if costs or benefits change a lot, it is updated and approved again. Precise terms: business case, alternatives analysis, benefit baseline, sensitivity analysis.

categories.Alternatives: Compare realistic options, including the do-nothing option, so approvers can see the best use of funds.
categories.Benefits: Measurable, with a baseline taken before the project and a named owner.
categories.Sensitivity analysis: Shows how the result changes if a key assumption, such as adoption rate, falls short.
categories.Mandatory projects: When a law or regulation requires the change, the obligation is the justification; the business case picks the lowest-cost, lowest-risk way to comply.

subtopics.key_point: Every promised benefit needs a measurable target, a measured starting baseline and a named business owner before approval. A materially changed business case goes back to the sponsors for re-approval.
common_mistakes: Approving a business case with benefits like "improved efficiency" that have no number, no baseline and no owner.
Treating the business case as finished once the project is approved.
subtopics.exam_tip: If a stem says costs rose or benefits shrank mid-project, the answer is to update the business case and get it re-approved, not to keep going because money is already spent.

subtopics.name: Feasibility Study and Build, Buy or Subscribe
subtopics.summary: Before committing, an organization checks whether the idea can actually work, from several angles, not just whether the technology exists. It then decides whether to build the system itself, buy a package, or rent a cloud service. That choice should rest on total cost over the system's life and how well each option fits the requirements. Precise terms: feasibility study, total cost of ownership (TCO), build vs buy vs software as a service (SaaS).

categories.Technical: Can it be built and run with available or obtainable technology and skills?
categories.Economic: Do the benefits justify the costs over the system's life?
categories.Legal and regulatory: Does it meet laws, contracts and privacy rules?
categories.Operational: Will people and processes actually use and support it?
categories.Schedule: Can it be delivered when the business needs it?

subtopics.key_point: A complete feasibility study looks at technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule feasibility before the go or no-go decision. Sourcing choices follow a business case built on TCO, fit, lock-in and risk.
common_mistakes: Comparing only purchase price instead of total cost of ownership over several years.
Letting team preference decide between building and buying.
subtopics.exam_tip: An answer that checks only technical feasibility, or picks an option because a vendor demo was impressive, is incomplete. Look for the multi-angle, evidence-based option.

subtopics.name: Money Measures and Investment Decisions
subtopics.summary: Different money measures answer different questions. Net present value asks what the whole investment is worth in today's dollars, while payback asks how fast you get your money back. When deciding whether to continue a troubled project, only future costs and benefits count; money already spent cannot be recovered either way. Precise terms: net present value (NPV), payback period, return on investment (ROI), internal rate of return (IRR), sunk cost.

categories.NPV: Discounts all future cash flows to today. Best for long-lived investments with large later benefits.
categories.Payback period: Time to recover the original outlay. Simple, but ignores everything after payback.
categories.ROI: Net gain as a percentage of the cost.
categories.IRR: The discount rate at which NPV equals zero; compared with the organization's required return.

subtopics.key_point: Continue-or-stop decisions compare forward costs and benefits against the alternatives and ignore sunk cost.
common_mistakes: Using payback to judge a project whose main benefits arrive in later years.
Counting money already spent as a reason to continue.
subtopics.exam_tip: "We have already spent too much to stop" is the sunk-cost trap. Also match the measure to the question: long-horizon value favors NPV, cash-tight quick recovery favors payback.

subtopics.name: Acquiring Software from Vendors
subtopics.summary: Buying software means choosing a supplier carefully and protecting yourself if that supplier fails. Requirements go out to vendors, answers are scored against agreed criteria, and the contract spells out service levels, audit rights and exit terms. For critical custom software, the vendor's source code can be held by a neutral third party in case the vendor goes out of business. Precise terms: request for proposal (RFP), vendor evaluation criteria, right to audit, source code escrow.
subtopics.key_point: Source code escrow protects continuity of business-critical software, but only if someone independently and periodically checks that the deposit is complete, current and builds the production version.
common_mistakes: Signing a contract with no right-to-audit or exit clause.
Assuming the escrow deposit is usable without ever testing a build from it.
subtopics.exam_tip: An escrow agreement on paper is not assurance. The stronger answer verifies the deposit. Also beware choosing the cheapest bid without scoring it against the requirements.

subtopics.name: Plan-Driven Models: Waterfall, Spiral and Prototyping
subtopics.summary: Some projects follow a fixed sequence: agree requirements, design, build, test, deploy, then maintain, with a sign-off gate between each step. That works well when requirements are stable and well understood. When risk or uncertainty is high, other models loop back to reduce risk or let users try a working model before the real build. Precise terms: waterfall, spiral model, prototyping, rapid application development (RAD).

categories.Waterfall: One phase finishes and is signed off before the next starts. Strong documentation; late changes are expensive.
categories.Spiral: Repeated cycles, each starting by finding and resolving the biggest risks before more effort is committed.
categories.Prototyping: Users interact with an early working model to firm up uncertain requirements. Risk: the prototype gets pushed into production without proper controls.
categories.RAD: Speed-focused delivery using prototypes, reusable components and close user involvement, often inside fixed timeboxes.

subtopics.key_point: Pick the model that fits the requirements and risk: stable requirements suit waterfall, uncertain requirements suit prototyping or iterative methods, and large high-risk work suits the spiral model.
common_mistakes: Choosing prototyping for a project with stable, fully known requirements.
Letting a prototype become the production system without readiness checks.
subtopics.exam_tip: No model removes the need for controls. Whatever the method, the auditor looks for approved requirements, testing evidence and sign-offs.

subtopics.name: Agile, Scrum and Kanban
subtopics.summary: Agile teams deliver small pieces of working software often and adjust as they learn. Scrum does this in fixed-length sprints with a set of regular meetings, while Kanban pulls work through a board continuously and limits how much is in progress at once. Agile still needs written records; it just keeps them lean. Precise terms: sprint, product backlog, velocity, work-in-progress (WIP) limit.

categories.Scrum: Time-boxed sprints, defined roles (product owner, Scrum Master, developers) and four events per sprint. Fits iterative product development.
categories.Kanban: Continuous flow with WIP limits and no fixed sprints. Fits support or operations work with shifting priorities.
categories.Velocity: Work completed per sprint. Useful for forecasting only after it stabilizes over several sprints.

subtopics.key_point: Agile means just-enough documentation, not none: design and control decisions must be recorded well enough to maintain and audit the system. Regulated projects can use agile when gates, signed baselines and traceability supply the evidence.
common_mistakes: Using a single sprint's velocity to promise a delivery date.
Leaving privacy and security checks until the end; in agile they belong in sprint planning before stories are committed.
subtopics.exam_tip: "Agile, so no documentation" is always a trap. Know the four Scrum events inside a sprint: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.

subtopics.name: DevOps, CI/CD and DevSecOps
subtopics.summary: DevOps joins the people who build software with the people who run it, and automates the path from code to production. Every change is built and tested automatically, and automated gates stop a release if tests or security scans fail. DevSecOps adds security to that same pipeline so problems are caught early, when they are cheap to fix. Precise terms: continuous integration (CI), continuous delivery, continuous deployment, quality gate, shift left.

categories.SAST: Static application security testing. Scans source code without running it; best on every pull request.
categories.SCA: Software composition analysis. Finds known vulnerabilities and license issues in open-source components; run on every build.
categories.Pipeline evidence: Tamper-evident logs linking each deployment to its approval, tests and scans.
categories.DORA metrics: Deployment frequency and lead time (speed) paired with change failure rate and time to restore (stability).

subtopics.key_point: Automated gates that block deployment on failed tests or scans give consistent, preventive assurance on every build. A well-built pipeline also produces the change evidence auditors need.
common_mistakes: Assuming frequent releases cannot be audited. Pipeline-generated evidence can make them more auditable than manual releases.
Sending scan results to a separate security team only. In DevSecOps, findings go into the delivery team's backlog with fix deadlines by severity.
subtopics.exam_tip: Continuous delivery keeps every build ready to release but a person decides when; continuous deployment releases automatically. Do not mix them up.

subtopics.name: Requirements, Traceability and Development Tools
subtopics.summary: Everything a system does should trace back to a requirement someone approved. A traceability matrix links each requirement to its design, code and tests, so nothing is missed and the effect of a change can be seen. Tools that generate code, including AI assistants, speed things up but do not change the rules. Precise terms: requirements baseline, requirements traceability matrix (RTM), behavior-driven development (BDD), code generator.
subtopics.key_point: Approved requirements are the baseline for every later phase. Generated or AI-assisted code is still source code and goes through the same review, testing and configuration management.
common_mistakes: Starting design before requirements are approved by the business.
Trusting AI-generated code without license scanning and rules about what data may be put in prompts.
subtopics.exam_tip: When asked how to prove every requirement was built and tested, the answer is the traceability matrix. Code from a tool skipping review is a trap.

subtopics.name: Deciding Which Controls a System Needs
subtopics.summary: Controls should be designed in from the start, because bolting them on after go-live is costly and weak. The starting point is a risk assessment: what data the system holds, how sensitive it is and what could go wrong. Frameworks help choose suitable controls, but the risk decides which ones are needed. Precise terms: control requirements, security by design, privacy by design, threat modeling.

categories.Threat modeling: A structured look at how the design could be attacked. STRIDE groups threats as spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.
categories.Security by design: Security requirements, such as phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, are written into requirements and design, not retrofitted.
categories.Privacy by design: Data flows, data minimization and consent are checked before features are built.

subtopics.key_point: During development the IS auditor advises on control requirements; management designs, implements and owns the controls. Control requirements come from risk assessment informed by data classification.
common_mistakes: Adding authentication strength after go-live instead of in the requirements.
Letting the auditor sign off the control design, which would impair later independence.
subtopics.exam_tip: Watch for answers where the auditor designs the controls (independence problem) or where a framework checklist replaces the risk assessment.

subtopics.name: Application Controls: Input, Processing, Output
subtopics.summary: Application controls follow the data through the system. Input controls check data before it is accepted, processing controls make sure it is handled correctly, and output controls make sure results are complete and reach the right people. Together they keep data complete, accurate, valid and unaltered. Precise terms: input controls, processing controls, output controls, data integrity.

categories.Input controls: Edit and validation checks (range, format, existence, check digit), authorization of transactions, batch totals.
categories.Processing controls: Run-to-run totals, reasonableness checks, limit checks during calculation, error handling and reprocessing rules.
categories.Output controls: Reconciling output to input totals, controlled distribution of reports, secure retention and disposal of output.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 430 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Application controls: input controls, processing controls, output controls'><rect x='8' y='24' width='112' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='64' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Input controls</text><rect x='142' y='24' width='140' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='212' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Processing controls</text><rect x='304' y='24' width='118' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='363' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Output controls</text><line x1='122' y1='46' x2='133' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M133,42 L140,46 L133,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='284' y1='46' x2='295' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M295,42 L302,46 L295,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Data enters, gets processed and comes out. Each stage has its own controls, and together they protect data integrity end to end.

subtopics.key_point: Stop bad data at the door: input controls validate that data is complete, accurate, valid and authorized before processing, which is cheaper than finding errors later.
common_mistakes: Calling an access control an input control. Access controls decide who may use the system; input controls check the data itself.
Relying on output review to catch errors that an input edit check could have blocked.
subtopics.exam_tip: Match the control to its stage. A range or check-digit test is an input control; a run-to-run total is a processing control; a distribution list check is an output control.

subtopics.name: Preventive, Automated and Built-In Controls
subtopics.summary: Controls either stop a problem before it happens or spot it afterward, and they are either done by the system or by a person. For high-volume, well-defined risks, a check built into the application works every time, while a person reviewing reports gets tired and misses things. Settings that change how the system behaves need the same care as code. Precise terms: preventive control, detective control, automated control, segregation of duties (SoD), configurable parameters.

categories.Preventive: Stops the error or misuse from happening, such as an edit check or a role that cannot both create and approve a payment.
categories.Detective: Finds it after the fact, such as an exception report or a log review.
categories.Corrective: Fixes the problem and its cause once detected.
categories.Compensating: A substitute control used when the preferred control is not practical.

subtopics.key_point: Prefer automated preventive controls for high-volume risks. Build segregation of duties into role design so the application blocks conflicting combinations instead of detecting misuse later.
common_mistakes: Assuming a detective control is as strong as a preventive one for routine transactions.
Leaving configuration tables open to anyone with admin access and no change log.
subtopics.exam_tip: A monthly manual review of conflicting access is weaker than a role design that prevents the conflict. Also, parameter tables (rates, limits, thresholds) need restricted access, approval and change logging.

subtopics.name: Audit Trails, Logging and Data Lineage
subtopics.summary: If something goes wrong, you need a reliable record of who did what and when. Logs should capture security-relevant events, be sent to a central place, use synchronized clocks and be protected from tampering. Lineage records show where each piece of data came from and how it changed along the way. Precise terms: audit trail, non-repudiation, log integrity, data lineage.
subtopics.key_point: Logs are only evidence if they are complete, centrally collected, time-synchronized and protected from alteration, and tied to authenticated identities so users cannot deny their actions.
common_mistakes: Logging everything but never deciding who reviews which events.
Using shared accounts, which breaks the link between an action and a person.
subtopics.exam_tip: Logs stored only on the server they describe, editable by its admins, are a classic weak answer. For lineage, automated capture beats hand-written documentation.

subtopics.name: Levels of Testing
subtopics.summary: Testing builds up from small pieces to the whole. First each piece is tested alone, then pieces are tested together, then the full system is tested, and finally business users confirm it does their job. Most automated tests should be the small, fast kind, with fewer big end-to-end ones. Precise terms: unit testing, integration testing, system testing, user acceptance testing (UAT), test pyramid.

categories.Unit: One module or function, usually by the developer.
categories.Integration: The interfaces and data passed between components.
categories.System: The complete system against functional and non-functional requirements.
categories.UAT: Business users confirm the system meets their needs, against criteria agreed in advance.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 408 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Testing levels: unit, integration, system, then user acceptance testing'><rect x='8' y='24' width='80' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='48' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Unit</text><rect x='110' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='156' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Integration</text><rect x='224' y='24' width='82' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='265' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>System</text><rect x='328' y='24' width='72' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='364' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>UAT</text><line x1='90' y1='46' x2='101' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M101,42 L108,46 L101,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='204' y1='46' x2='215' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M215,42 L222,46 L215,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='308' y1='46' x2='319' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M319,42 L326,46 L319,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Testing grows in scope: one unit, then units working together, then the whole system, then the business users' acceptance.

subtopics.key_point: Each level has its own purpose, and UAT is the business owner's acceptance: it follows successful system testing and comes before cutover, in a production-like environment.
common_mistakes: Letting the development team run and sign off UAT on the business's behalf.
Building a suite of mostly slow end-to-end tests and few unit tests.
subtopics.exam_tip: If the question is about interfaces between modules, the answer is integration testing, not unit or system testing. If it is about whether the business accepts the system, it is UAT.

subtopics.name: Test Types and Techniques
subtopics.summary: Beyond the levels, tests have different goals. Some check that old features still work after a change, some push the system with heavy load, and some try to break in. When time is short, test the riskiest areas hardest. Precise terms: regression testing, performance testing, security testing, black-box and white-box testing, boundary-value analysis, risk-based testing.

categories.Regression: Re-runs existing tests to confirm a change did not break what already worked.
categories.Load / stress / soak: Load confirms expected volume, stress finds the breaking point, soak runs for a long time to expose leaks and slow degradation.
categories.DAST / IAST / RASP: DAST probes the running app from outside, IAST instruments it during testing, RASP protects it from inside in production.
categories.Black box / white box: Black box tests behavior without seeing code; white box tests the internal logic and paths.

subtopics.key_point: Risk-based testing puts effort where failure would hurt most and is most likely. Coverage figures show what code ran, not whether the tests would catch a defect.
common_mistakes: Skipping regression testing for a "small" change.
Treating a high coverage percentage as proof the system is well tested.
subtopics.exam_tip: High code coverage alone does not prove good tests; mutation testing checks whether tests actually catch injected faults. Boundary-value tests sit on and either side of each limit.

subtopics.name: Test Environments and Test Data
subtopics.summary: Tests are only as believable as the place they run and the data they use. The test environment should be separate from production but close to it in size and setup, or performance results mean little. Real customer data copied into testing must be disguised first so it is not exposed. Precise terms: production-like environment, environment segregation, data masking, pseudonymization.
subtopics.key_point: Mask or pseudonymize production-derived data before it leaves production, so non-production environments never hold real personal data. Performance results count only when the test environment matches production volume, tier and load.
common_mistakes: Giving developers live customer data for convenience.
Load testing on a small server and assuming production will scale the same way.
subtopics.exam_tip: Masking the data after it is already copied into test is too late. Testing in production itself is another trap.

subtopics.name: Go-Live Readiness and Acceptance
subtopics.summary: Going live is a management decision based on evidence, not a date on a calendar. Clear, measurable acceptance criteria are agreed before testing starts, and owners sign off that they have been met. Any serious open issue is either fixed first or knowingly accepted by the person who owns the risk. Precise terms: exit criteria, go/no-go decision, risk acceptance, certification and accreditation.

categories.Acceptance criteria: Measurable, tied to business requirements, agreed by the business owner and fixed before testing starts.
categories.Cutover rehearsal: Staged dress rehearsals of technical and business steps, with time left to fix what they reveal.
categories.Certification: Technical assessment of whether controls meet requirements.
categories.Accreditation (authorization): An authorized official accepts the residual risk and approves operation.

subtopics.key_point: Go-live rests on readiness criteria signed off by accountable owners. High-risk findings are fixed before go-live or formally accepted by the risk owner; the auditor recommends, management decides.
common_mistakes: Letting the IS auditor approve or block go-live. The auditor reports and recommends; management owns the decision.
Writing acceptance criteria after testing has started.
subtopics.exam_tip: Under deadline pressure, the right answer ships a fully tested smaller scope with documented risk acceptance; skipping or shortening testing quietly is wrong. Certification is the technical evaluation; accreditation is management accepting residual risk.

subtopics.name: Configuration Management and Baselines
subtopics.summary: Configuration management keeps track of exactly which versions of everything make up a working system. Code, designs, requirements, scripts, settings and builds are all recorded, and an approved set becomes the baseline that changes are measured against. Infrastructure and database changes are written as versioned scripts and go through the same review as code. Precise terms: configuration item (CI), baseline, version control, infrastructure as code, GitOps.

categories.Configuration item: Any component that must be controlled: code, design, requirement, build, script, configuration file.
categories.Branching: Short-lived branches merged often through reviewed pull requests support continuous integration.
categories.Feature flags: Need owners, versioned definitions, retirement dates and logged, authorized changes.

subtopics.key_point: Everything that defines the system is a configuration item under formal change control, including database schema changes, environment definitions and feature flags.
common_mistakes: Treating only source code as a configuration item.
Leaving old feature flags in place with no owner.
subtopics.exam_tip: Direct, manual edits to production databases or servers bypass configuration management. In GitOps, Git holds the approved desired state and an agent continuously corrects drift.

subtopics.name: Change and Release Management
subtopics.summary: Every change to production should be requested, assessed, approved, tested and then released by someone other than the person who wrote it. Big or risky changes are reviewed by a change board that weighs impact and readiness. Emergency fixes may move faster, but they are still documented and approved after the fact. Precise terms: change request, change advisory board (CAB), emergency change, segregation of duties between development and production.

categories.Normal change: Assessed and authorized case by case; significant ones go to the CAB.
categories.Emergency change: Fast-tracked to fix an urgent problem; documented and reviewed afterward.

subtopics.key_point: Developers should not move their own code into production. The CAB assesses risk, impact and readiness and advises the change authority; it does not plan or carry out the change.
common_mistakes: Approving changes based on the requester's assurance instead of test evidence.
Letting many teams release independently without checking the interfaces between them.
subtopics.exam_tip: An emergency change with no after-the-fact review is the trap. So is a developer with standing write access to production "for support".

subtopics.name: Deployment Strategies and Rollback
subtopics.summary: How a release reaches users can limit the damage if something is wrong. A canary release sends a small share of real traffic to the new version first and widens it only while health checks stay good. Every release needs a tested way back that restores data and settings, not just the old code. Precise terms: canary release, blue-green deployment, rollback plan, roll forward.

categories.Canary: Small slice of live traffic first; expand only while signals hold.
categories.Blue-green: Two identical environments; switch traffic to the new one and switch back if needed.
categories.Error budget: In site reliability engineering, when the allowed unreliability is used up, non-essential releases pause until reliability recovers.

subtopics.key_point: If a staged rollout starts failing, halt it and follow the rollback playbook first, then investigate the cause. A rollback plan must be tested, time-bound and restore data and configuration consistency.
common_mistakes: Having a rollback plan that was never rehearsed.
Investigating the root cause while a bad release keeps spreading to more regions.
subtopics.exam_tip: If rolling back would destroy data the new release has already written, preserve that data first, then restore service by hotfix or roll forward. Rolling back blindly is the trap.

subtopics.name: Software Supply Chain Integrity
subtopics.summary: Modern systems are built from many outside components, so you need to know what is inside and be sure nothing was swapped along the way. A parts list of every component and version lets you find affected systems fast when a flaw is announced. Signing each build and checking the signature before deployment proves where it came from. Precise terms: software bill of materials (SBOM), artifact signing, provenance, open-source license compliance.
subtopics.key_point: Know your components and prove your builds: keep an SBOM, sign artifacts at build time and verify signatures before deployment.
common_mistakes: Signing images but never checking the signature at deployment.
Ignoring license terms of open-source components.
subtopics.exam_tip: An SBOM lists components; it does not by itself fix vulnerabilities. Strong-copyleft licenses can oblige you to release your own code, so licenses are tracked, scanned before merge, and copyleft components isolated.

topics.topic_name: System Migration, Infrastructure Deployment, and Data Conversion

subtopics.name: Cutover Strategies
subtopics.summary: Cutover is the moment users switch from the old system to the new one, and there are several ways to do it. You can run both side by side and compare, switch one group or one location first, switch in waves, or switch everyone at once. The safer approaches cost more time and effort, so the choice depends on risk. Precise terms: parallel run, pilot, phased cutover, direct (big-bang) cutover, fallback plan.

categories.Parallel run: Old and new run together and results are reconciled. Best evidence, highest cost.
categories.Pilot: One site or group goes first to prove the system before wider rollout.
categories.Phased: The system is introduced in stages, by module or business unit.
categories.Direct (big bang): Everyone switches at once. Fast and cheap, but no easy way back if it fails.

subtopics.key_point: Choose the cutover approach by risk and complexity, and always have a tested fallback. When cutover checks show an unexplained material problem, stop at the decision gate and let management proceed or fall back on the evidence.
common_mistakes: Choosing big bang for a complex, high-impact system to save time.
Having a fallback plan that depends on a legacy system already switched off.
subtopics.exam_tip: Parallel running gives the strongest comparison evidence but costs the most. Phased cutover suits large, multi-unit replacements because each wave limits the damage. Pushing on past an unexplained variance is the trap.

subtopics.name: Data Conversion Controls
subtopics.summary: Moving data into a new system is where records quietly go missing or change meaning. The business owner of the data approves how old fields map to new ones, and dirty data is cleaned before loading, with the owner approving each fix. Afterward, totals are compared on both sides and every difference is explained. Precise terms: data mapping, data cleansing, reconciliation, control totals, record counts.

categories.Record counts: Number of records extracted, loaded and rejected must add up.
categories.Control totals: Sums of key amount fields match between source and target.
categories.Hash totals: Sums of non-financial fields (such as account numbers) to show nothing was altered.
categories.Key cross-reference: Retained mapping from legacy keys to new keys, plus conversion logs, for audit trail.

subtopics.key_point: Conversion integrity is proven by source-to-target reconciliation of record counts and control totals, with variances investigated. Mapping rules and cleansing decisions are approved by the data owner, not IT alone.
common_mistakes: Letting IT decide mapping rules for business data.
Cleaning data after it is loaded into the live system.
subtopics.exam_tip: Spot-checking a few records is weaker than full reconciliation of counts and totals. Keep a cross-reference from each old key to its new key so any converted record can be traced back.

subtopics.name: Infrastructure Deployment and Migration Planning
subtopics.summary: The new platform must be secure and ready before any real data moves onto it. Systems that depend on each other are mapped first, so they move together in planned waves. The old system is only switched off once the final checks are signed off and its records are safely archived. Precise terms: security baseline, dependency mapping, migration waves, decommissioning, data retention.
subtopics.key_point: Verify the target infrastructure against its approved security baseline before loading production data, and confirm legal and contractual retention needs are met before any irreversible migration step.
common_mistakes: Hardening the new servers after production data is already on them.
Dropping historical records that must be kept for regulatory reasons.
subtopics.exam_tip: Decommissioning the legacy system right after go-live, before final reconciliation sign-off and archiving, is the trap. So is migrating systems one by one without knowing their dependencies.

subtopics.name: Purpose and Timing of the Review
subtopics.summary: Some time after go-live, the organization asks a simple question: did we get what we paid for? The review compares the real results with the benefits promised in the business case and checks that the system works as designed. It waits until the system has run steadily for a while, so the numbers are real and not distorted by start-up problems. Precise terms: post-implementation review (PIR), benefits realization.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 476 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Post-implementation review happens after the system goes live and settles in'><rect x='8' y='24' width='120' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='68' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>System goes live</text><rect x='150' y='24' width='120' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='210' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Settle-in period</text><rect x='292' y='24' width='176' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='380' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Post-implementation review</text><line x1='130' y1='46' x2='141' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M141,42 L148,46 L141,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='272' y1='46' x2='283' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M283,42 L290,46 L283,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Go live, let the system settle, then review. Waiting for stable operation means benefits and controls are judged on real data.

subtopics.key_point: The primary purpose of a post-implementation review is to compare realized benefits against the approved business case, once the system has operated stably long enough to measure.
common_mistakes: Treating the review as a technical bug hunt instead of a benefits check.
Scheduling it so early that only start-up issues are visible.
subtopics.exam_tip: A review the day after go-live is too early; one years later is too late to act. Review effort should also scale with the size and risk of the change, as defined in policy.

subtopics.name: What the IS Auditor Looks At
subtopics.summary: The auditor's main contribution is checking whether the controls designed into the system actually work now that it is live. Evidence matters: measured data compared with the starting baseline beats opinions or surveys. When users invent workarounds, that usually means a designed control is missing or broken. Precise terms: control objective attainment, objective evidence, reviewer independence, control gap.

categories.Controls: Do the input, processing, output and access controls work as designed?
categories.Benefits: Are results measured against a pre-project baseline?
categories.Workarounds: Report them as control gaps so management assigns an owner and fix date.
categories.Independence: Someone other than the delivery team performs or leads the review.

subtopics.key_point: The IS auditor gives assurance on whether controls work in live operation and meet their objectives, using objective evidence. The reviewer must be objective, so the team that delivered the system should not review itself.
common_mistakes: Accepting the project manager's statement that benefits were achieved.
Recommending more training for low adoption before checking why users avoid the system.
subtopics.exam_tip: Low adoption or user complaints are symptoms; find the root cause before recommending a fix. A missing benefit baseline means benefits cannot be proven, which is itself a finding.

subtopics.name: Acting on the Results
subtopics.summary: A review is useful only if its findings lead to action. Each recommendation gets an owner, a due date and tracked status until it is closed. If benefits fall short, the business sponsor who promised them owns the plan to close the gap, and lessons feed the next project. Precise terms: follow-up, remediation tracking, benefit shortfall, lessons learned.
subtopics.key_point: Benefits realization is a business responsibility: the sponsor owns the plan to close any shortfall. The auditor recommends and follows up; management decides and acts.
common_mistakes: Issuing recommendations without follow-up.
Assigning the benefit gap to the project manager after the project has closed.
subtopics.exam_tip: An answer that has the auditor or IT fix the benefit shortfall is a trap. So is a report with no named owners or dates.

key_terminologies.Project charter: Sponsor-approved document that formally authorizes a project and gives the project manager authority over its resources.
key_terminologies.Project sponsor: Senior business owner who funds the project and is accountable for its benefits.
key_terminologies.Steering committee: Group of senior decision makers who govern a project and resolve issues beyond the project manager's authority.
key_terminologies.Critical path: The longest chain of dependent tasks; it sets the shortest possible project duration and has no slack.
key_terminologies.Earned value management (EVM): Tracks cost and schedule by comparing the value of work done with planned value and actual cost.
key_terminologies.Management reserve: Budget held outside the cost baseline for unknown risks; drawing on it needs sponsor or steering committee approval.
key_terminologies.Function point analysis: Sizes software by the functions it delivers, independent of programming language.
key_terminologies.Business case: The justification for an investment, comparing options and stating measurable, owned benefits.
key_terminologies.Feasibility study: Assessment of whether a proposal is technically, economically, legally, operationally and schedule feasible.
key_terminologies.Net present value (NPV): Value today of all future cash flows of an investment, after discounting.
key_terminologies.Sunk cost: Money already spent that cannot be recovered and should not drive a continue-or-stop decision.
key_terminologies.Source code escrow: Arrangement where a neutral party holds a vendor's source code for release if the vendor fails.
key_terminologies.Waterfall: Sequential development model in which each phase is completed and signed off before the next begins.
key_terminologies.Agile: Iterative approach delivering working software in short cycles with lean but sufficient documentation.
key_terminologies.CI/CD: Automated pipeline that integrates, tests and prepares or releases every code change.
key_terminologies.Requirements traceability matrix: Table linking each requirement to its design, code and tests.
key_terminologies.Input controls: Checks that data is complete, accurate, valid and authorized before processing.
key_terminologies.Segregation of duties: Splitting conflicting tasks between people or roles so no one can commit and hide an error or fraud alone.
key_terminologies.Unit testing: Testing a single module or function in isolation.
key_terminologies.Integration testing: Testing the interfaces and data flow between components.
key_terminologies.User acceptance testing (UAT): Business users confirm the system meets their needs against pre-agreed criteria before cutover.
key_terminologies.Regression testing: Re-running existing tests to confirm a change did not break existing functions.
key_terminologies.Data masking: Disguising sensitive values in copied data so test environments hold no real personal data.
key_terminologies.Configuration item: Any controlled component of a system, such as code, design, requirement, script or build.
key_terminologies.Change advisory board (CAB): Group that assesses the risk, impact and readiness of significant changes before authorization.
key_terminologies.Canary release: Releasing to a small share of live traffic first and expanding only while health signals hold.
key_terminologies.Software bill of materials (SBOM): Inventory of the components and versions inside a piece of software.
key_terminologies.Parallel run: Running old and new systems together and reconciling their results before switching over.
key_terminologies.Control totals: Sums of key fields compared between source and target to prove data was transferred completely and accurately.
key_terminologies.Post-implementation review: Review after stable operation that compares realized benefits with the business case and checks that controls work.

domains.domain_name: Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience
domains.summary: This domain is about keeping IT running day to day and getting it back when something goes badly wrong. Part A covers operations: the components systems run on, assets, scheduled jobs, interfaces, user-built tools, availability and capacity, incidents and problems, changes and patches, logs, service levels and databases. Part B covers resilience: working out what matters most, designing systems that tolerate failure, backups, and the continuity and disaster recovery plans that bring the business back.
domains.real_life_analogy: Think of running a busy airport. Day to day, ground staff follow a schedule, maintenance crews log every repair, nothing moves on the airfield without clearance, and the control tower records every instruction. That is IT operations. The airport also plans for the day a runway closes: it knows which flights matter most, how long it can cope with delays before passengers are stranded, which nearby airport takes diverted flights, and it rehearses those plans before it needs them. That is business resilience.

topics.summary: The physical and logical parts that business systems run on: networks, operating systems, utilities and hardware. The auditor's question is always the same: is each component configured, supported and changed under control?

subtopics.name: Network Building Blocks
subtopics.summary: A network is the road system that lets computers reach each other. A local network links devices in one building or campus, and a wide-area network links distant sites. Switches move traffic inside a network, routers move it between networks, and firewalls decide which traffic is allowed at all. Precise term: network infrastructure, the devices and services (switches, routers, firewalls, load balancers, DNS) that carry and govern traffic between systems.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 364 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='DNS translates a domain name into the IP address a computer connects to'><rect x='8' y='24' width='104' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='60' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>example.com</text><rect x='134' y='24' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='184' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>DNS lookup</text><rect x='256' y='24' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='306' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>IP address</text><line x1='114' y1='46' x2='125' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M125,42 L132,46 L125,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='236' y1='46' x2='247' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M247,42 L254,46 L247,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Name to number. A DNS lookup turns the name a person types into the IP address the network actually routes to. If DNS fails, working systems look unreachable; if it is tampered with, users can be sent somewhere else.

categories.Switch: Connects devices within one network segment.
categories.Firewall: Allows or blocks traffic according to a rule set.
categories.Load balancer: Spreads requests across several servers; a shared production component.
categories.NAT: Rewrites private internal addresses to public ones at the boundary.
categories.DNS: Turns names people type into the numeric addresses computers use.

subtopics.key_point: Network devices are production infrastructure. Their configurations belong under change control, and the running configuration is compared with an approved baseline so unauthorized changes show up.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an answer that says a router or switch "secures" the network. Forwarding traffic is not the same as enforcing policy; firewalls permit or deny flows by rule. Also watch for IPv6 left enabled but uninspected, which opens a parallel, unfiltered path.

subtopics.name: OSI and TCP/IP Reference Models
subtopics.summary: Reference models split network communication into layers so each job can be described on its own. The OSI model has seven layers, from cabling at the bottom to applications at the top. The TCP/IP model used on the internet has four, and its single application layer covers the top three OSI layers. Precise term: layered reference model, a framework that assigns each communication function to a layer that serves the one above it.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='OSI model seven-layer pyramid from Physical at the base to Application at the peak'><rect x='135' y='10' width='130' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='32' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>7 · Application</text><rect x='115' y='50' width='170' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='72' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>6 · Presentation</text><rect x='95' y='90' width='210' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='112' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>5 · Session</text><rect x='75' y='130' width='250' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='152' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>4 · Transport</text><rect x='55' y='170' width='290' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='192' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>3 · Network</text><rect x='35' y='210' width='330' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='232' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>2 · Data Link</text><rect x='15' y='250' width='370' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='200' y='272' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='12' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>1 · Physical</text></svg>
illustration.caption: The seven OSI layers, from Physical at the base to Application at the top. Layers 1 to 4 move data across the network; layers 5 to 7 prepare it for the application.

subtopics.key_point: Map a control to the layer where it works. Transport stays its own layer in both models; only OSI layers 5 to 7 merge into the TCP/IP application layer.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: folding the transport layer into the TCP/IP application layer. TCP and UDP sit in a separate transport layer in both models.
subtopics.memory_aid: Bottom to top: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" for Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

subtopics.name: Operating Systems and Utility Programs
subtopics.summary: The operating system is the base layer every application runs on, so a weak OS weakens everything above it. Systems ship with vendor defaults that favor convenience, not security. Utility programs are powerful admin tools that can read or change data directly, skipping the checks an application would apply. Precise term: hardened configuration baseline, the approved, documented secure settings an OS must match.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Operating system controls: access control, audit logging, patch management, privileged accounts'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Access control</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Audit logging</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Patch management</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Privileged accounts</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Four core OS controls: access control, audit logging, patching and privileged-account management. Because the OS sits under every application, these controls protect everything above it.

subtopics.key_point: Harden from a baseline, monitor for drift, and restrict utilities to named administrators with least privilege. Where a server class cannot meet the baseline, use a formal exception with compensating controls and risk acceptance.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: treating antivirus as proof that system files are intact. Antivirus finds known malicious code; file integrity monitoring detects any change against a trusted baseline.

subtopics.name: Hardware Maintenance and End of Support
subtopics.summary: Hardware wears out and vendors eventually stop supporting it. Good maintenance watches health data and failure trends, so parts are replaced in planned windows instead of during an outage. Once a product reaches end of support, no more fixes arrive, and the risk grows each month. Precise term: end of support (EOS), the date after which a vendor no longer provides fixes, parts or help.
subtopics.key_point: Running unsupported hardware is a business risk decision. The accountable owner formally accepts the residual risk, with compensating controls or extended support and a dated replacement plan.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: "we have redundancy, so maintenance is less urgent." Redundancy reduces the impact of a failure, not how often failures happen. Also, a future replacement plan does not lower today's exposure.

topics.summary: You cannot protect, patch, license or recover what you do not know you own. Asset management keeps an accurate, owned record of every asset across its whole life.

subtopics.name: Asset Inventory and the CMDB
subtopics.summary: An asset inventory lists the hardware, software, cloud resources and data the organization relies on, with an owner for each. A configuration management database (CMDB) goes further and records how those items connect. Records drift quickly, especially in the cloud, where resources appear and disappear in minutes. Precise term: IT asset lifecycle, the stages from acquisition and assignment through change to secure disposal.
subtopics.key_point: An inventory is only a control if it stays accurate. Define scope and owners first, then keep the record current through automated discovery and regular reconciliation.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: trusting purchase records or a one-time survey as the inventory. For cloud estates, the reliable answer is continuous discovery through the provider's APIs, tied to enforced ownership tags.

subtopics.name: Software Licensing
subtopics.summary: Every installed copy of software must be covered by a license the organization actually holds. Installing more copies than you paid for creates legal and financial exposure. Open-source licenses carry duties too: some require that changes you distribute be shared under the same terms. Precise term: license compliance, reconciling discovered installations against purchased entitlements and license terms.

categories.Proprietary: Use is limited by the vendor's contract and counts of seats or cores.
categories.Copyleft open source: Distributed derivatives must use the same license terms.

subtopics.key_point: Compliance is proven by comparing what is installed with what is owned. Purchase records alone show only what was bought.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: ignoring open-source terms. A copyleft license such as the GPL can require a distributed derivative product to be released under the same license, which can expose proprietary code.

subtopics.name: Secure Disposal and Media Sanitization
subtopics.summary: When equipment or media is retired, the data on it must not leave with it. The right method depends on how sensitive the data is and whether the media will leave the organization's control. After sanitizing, someone checks it worked and keeps a record. Precise term: media sanitization, making data on media unrecoverable by clearing, purging or destroying it (as set out in NIST SP 800-88).

categories.Clear: Overwrite so ordinary tools cannot recover data; for reuse inside the organization.
categories.Purge: Techniques that defeat even lab-grade recovery; for media leaving control.
categories.Destroy: Physically ruin the media so it cannot be used again.

subtopics.key_point: Match the method to the data's sensitivity and the media's destination, then verify and document the result.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: assuming deletion or formatting removes data. In shared cloud storage you cannot shred a disk, so destroying customer-managed encryption keys (cryptographic erase) is the practical method, with the logged key destruction as evidence.

topics.topic_name: Job Scheduling and Production Process Automation
topics.summary: Production work such as overnight batches, interfaces and software robots runs without a person watching each step. Automation removes manual errors, but only if the schedule itself is authorized and the results are checked.

subtopics.name: Job Scheduling Controls
subtopics.summary: Scheduling software runs production jobs in the right order, waits for each dependency and reports what happened. That removes the risk of an operator starting jobs by hand in the wrong sequence. But a job that says "completed" may still have processed the wrong number of records. Precise term: job scheduler, software that launches production jobs by time and dependency and records outcomes.
subtopics.key_point: Changes to the schedule go through change control, and the people who maintain schedules are not the ones who approve production changes. Record counts and control totals, not just completion status, should gate the next job.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: reviewing only failure logs. An unauthorized or mis-sequenced job can run successfully and never appear as a failure; compare the schedule with approved business requirements instead.
common_mistakes: Accepting a bypass of the scheduler during busy periods such as year end. Close the bypass first, then assess what ran through it.
Letting urgent schedule changes skip change control. Use the emergency route, which still requires authorization and later review.

subtopics.name: Batch Monitoring, Restart and Rerun
subtopics.summary: Batches fail partway through, and a careless rerun can skip records or process them twice. Checkpoints let a job resume from a known point, and control totals confirm nothing was lost or doubled. Deadline alerts warn when a long-running batch might spill into business hours. Precise term: restart and rerun procedures, documented steps for resuming a failed job without duplication or omission.
subtopics.key_point: Recovery from a failed batch must protect completeness and accuracy; prove it with checkpoints and reconciled totals.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: "rerun the whole job from the start" as the safe choice. Without controls, a full rerun can post the same transactions twice.

subtopics.name: Robotic Process Automation (RPA)
subtopics.summary: Software robots (bots) copy what a person would do on screen, such as keying data from one system into another. Because they act fast and at scale, a bad bot can do a lot of damage quietly. Bots need the same discipline as any user and any program. Precise term: RPA bot, software that runs rule-based tasks through application interfaces on behalf of the business.
subtopics.key_point: Give each bot its own identity with least-privilege access and a named business owner. Treat bot logic as production code: tested, approved and promoted under change control.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: letting a bot run under a shared or personal human account. That breaks accountability, because no one can tell which actions the bot took.

topics.summary: Interfaces move data between systems, often in bulk and without people looking at it. The risk is data that arrives incomplete, changed, duplicated or not at all, with no one noticing.

subtopics.name: Where Interface Risk Sits
subtopics.summary: Data passing between systems can go wrong at several points: when the sender extracts it, while it travels, when middleware reformats it, and when the receiver loads it. An audit that looks only at one end misses the others. Precise term: system interface, an automated link that transfers data from one application to another, directly or through middleware.

categories.Middleware: Mapping or format errors change values.
categories.Receiver: Rejected, duplicated or partly loaded records.

subtopics.key_point: Scope follows the data end to end, from source to final posting, including any transformation in between.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: testing only the sending system because it "owns" the data. Many silent losses happen in middleware mapping or at the receiving end.

subtopics.name: Interface Controls
subtopics.summary: The receiving side should prove it got everything that was sent. That means comparing record counts and money totals with the sender's, and following up every difference. Interfaces that retry automatically also need a way to spot repeats, such as unique message numbers. Precise term: control totals, summary figures (counts, sums, hashes) compared at each end to prove completeness and accuracy.
subtopics.key_point: Reconcile at the receiving end and act on exceptions. Prevent duplicates before posting with unique identifiers or sequence checks; reconciliation only finds them afterwards.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: "the interface job finished successfully" as evidence. Job status does not show records were complete. Patches to connected systems should also include regression testing of dependent interfaces.

topics.summary: Business users build their own tools and sign up for their own services. That speeds work up, but those tools often skip the controls IT systems have, even when they feed critical numbers.

subtopics.name: End-User Computing (EUC)
subtopics.summary: End-user computing means tools built by business staff rather than IT, such as spreadsheets, small databases, scripts and, more and more, AI-generated logic. Some become critical without anyone deciding they should, for example a spreadsheet that calculates regulatory figures. Precise term: end-user computing (EUC), applications developed and run by business users outside formal IT development.
subtopics.key_point: Start with an owned inventory ranked by criticality, then apply controls proportional to risk. Critical tools need independent review of logic changes, version control, restricted access and testing, or migration to an IT-managed platform.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: letting owners rate their own tools' risk. Risk tiers need defined criteria and independent checking. Under a deadline, run the proven existing model with independent review instead of an untested rebuild.
common_mistakes: Assuming AI-assisted formulas or scripts need less review. They need the same independent testing as any logic feeding critical reporting.

subtopics.name: Shadow IT and Shadow AI
subtopics.summary: Shadow IT is technology used without IT's knowledge or approval, such as a team paying for its own cloud file service. Shadow AI is the same thing with AI tools, often with staff pasting sensitive data into them. You cannot find it by asking people; you find it in the traffic. Precise term: shadow IT, hardware, software or cloud services used for business without sanctioned approval.
subtopics.key_point: Discover it through independent telemetry such as proxy logs or a cloud access security broker (CASB). Then risk-rank each service and sanction and secure it, migrate it, or retire it.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an outright ban as the "strongest" answer. If the tool meets a real need, banning drives it further underground. For shadow AI, the first step is an acceptable-use rule for data plus a sanctioned alternative.

topics.summary: Availability is whether users can use a service when they need it. Capacity management makes sure enough computing resources exist before demand arrives.

subtopics.name: Availability and Its Measures
subtopics.summary: A service is available when users can actually complete their work on it, not just when a server is switched on. Availability should be measured the way users experience it, across every component in the path. Two measures explain it: how often things break and how quickly they are fixed. Precise term: availability, the share of agreed service time during which the service works as required.

categories.MTBF: Average running time between failures; higher is better.
categories.MTTR: Average time to restore after a failure; lower is better.
categories.End-to-end availability: Measured across the full transaction path as the user sees it.

subtopics.key_point: Availability targets come from business impact and tolerance for downtime, and are measured end to end against the hours the business needs the service. Exclusions must be agreed and limited.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: confusing MTBF and MTTR. MTBF (mean time between failures) shows reliability; MTTR (mean time to repair or restore) shows recovery speed. Availability depends on both.

subtopics.name: Capacity Management
subtopics.summary: Capacity management looks at how much processing, storage and network the business uses today and how much it will need tomorrow. It plans additions early enough to cover purchase and setup lead times. It also looks for ways to reduce or move demand before buying more. Precise term: capacity management, monitoring, forecasting and planning resources so performance targets are met cost-effectively.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 396 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Capacity management: monitor usage, forecast demand, provision capacity ahead of need'><rect x='8' y='24' width='104' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='60' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Monitor usage</text><rect x='134' y='24' width='116' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='192' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Forecast demand</text><rect x='272' y='24' width='116' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='330' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Provision ahead</text><line x1='114' y1='46' x2='125' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M125,42 L132,46 L125,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='252' y1='46' x2='263' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M263,42 L270,46 L263,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: The capacity cycle: watch usage, forecast demand, then add capacity before it is needed, so a shortfall never turns into an outage.

subtopics.key_point: Monitoring is only a control when someone reviews results against thresholds and trends lead to planned action. Plan for peaks, not averages, and try demand management before adding resources.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: assuming the cloud has unlimited capacity. Autoscaling stops at the provider's service quotas, so cloud capacity planning must track those limits. A soft quota can usually be raised by asking the provider.

topics.summary: Incident management gets users working again as fast as possible. Problem management finds and removes the underlying cause so the same incident does not keep coming back.

subtopics.name: Incident Management and the Service Desk
subtopics.summary: An incident is any unplanned interruption or drop in service quality, like an email system that stops sending. The service desk logs it, sets its priority and works toward restoring service, using a workaround if needed. It is closed only when the user confirms things work. Precise term: incident management, the process of restoring normal service as quickly as possible and limiting business impact.
subtopics.key_point: Priority reflects business impact and urgency. Restore service first; the root cause is pursued separately through problem management and is never simply skipped.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: measuring the help desk by speed or ticket volume alone. Outcome measures such as first-contact resolution and reopen rates show whether it is effective. Help desk staff must also escalate calls that look like security incidents.
common_mistakes: Resetting privileged credentials on a caller's word. Help-desk resets for privileged accounts need out-of-band identity verification.
Running a major outage without one incident commander. Concurrent incidents need one coordinator, with a separate liaison giving scheduled stakeholder updates.

subtopics.name: Handling Incidents in Sequence
subtopics.summary: When something abnormal happens, the order of steps matters. You first notice and record it, then stop it from spreading, then remove the cause, then restore normal operation, and finally learn from it. Jumping straight to the fix while the problem is still spreading makes the damage bigger. Precise term: incident handling lifecycle, the ordered stages of detection, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident review.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 580 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Incident handling lifecycle: detect, contain, eradicate, recover, lessons learned'><rect x='8' y='24' width='90' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='53' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Detection</text><rect x='120' y='24' width='104' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='172' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Containment</text><rect x='246' y='24' width='98' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='295' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Eradication</text><rect x='366' y='24' width='82' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='407' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Recovery</text><rect x='470' y='24' width='102' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='521' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Lessons learned</text><line x1='100' y1='46' x2='111' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M111,42 L118,46 L111,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='226' y1='46' x2='237' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M237,42 L244,46 L237,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='346' y1='46' x2='357' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M357,42 L364,46 L357,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='450' y1='46' x2='461' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M461,42 L468,46 L461,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: The incident lifecycle runs left to right. Containment sits before eradication on purpose, and the closing lessons-learned review is the step that stops the next incident but is the one most often skipped.

subtopics.key_point: Containment comes first: limit the damage before eradicating the cause. Decision rights are pre-delegated to an incident commander so response does not wait for executives.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an option that investigates root cause or collects perfect evidence while the attack or outage is still spreading. Contain first, then investigate.

subtopics.name: Problem Management and Root Cause Analysis
subtopics.summary: When the same kind of incident keeps returning, there is a deeper cause. Problem management looks for it using facts such as timelines and logs. If the cause is known but not yet fixed, it is logged with a workaround so the service desk can resolve repeat incidents quickly. Precise term: known error, a problem with a documented root cause and workaround that has not yet been permanently fixed.
subtopics.key_point: Recurring incidents signal a problem. Find the common root cause before choosing a permanent fix, and report trends by business impact so management can act.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: stopping at "human error." Good root cause analysis asks what process, tool or procedure weakness let the error happen. Post-incident reviews should be blameless and fact-based.

topics.topic_name: IT Change, Configuration, and Patch Management
topics.summary: Most outages and many security gaps start with a change. These processes make sure every change is authorized, tested, recorded and reversible.

subtopics.name: Change Management
subtopics.summary: Every change to production (code, settings, schedules, infrastructure) should be requested, assessed, approved, tested and recorded. The person who wrote a change should not be the one who moves it into production. Emergencies still happen, so there is a faster route with checks afterwards. Precise term: change management (also called change enablement), the process that assesses and authorizes each change to production.
subtopics.key_point: No unauthorized change reaches production. Separate development from deployment, require a tested backout plan, and review emergency changes independently soon after they are made.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: "it was urgent, so no approval was needed." Emergency changes may skip prior approval, but they still need independent review and approval shortly after implementation.
common_mistakes: When a release causes harm and a validated prior version exists, back it out through emergency change first; investigate root cause afterwards.

subtopics.name: Configuration Management
subtopics.summary: Configuration management records how each system is supposed to be set up and keeps checking that it still is. The approved setup is a baseline. Comparing the live settings with the baseline catches changes nobody logged, and source code gets the same care in one access-controlled repository with full history. Precise term: configuration baseline, the approved set of settings against which actual configurations are compared.
subtopics.key_point: Detect unauthorized change by comparing actual configurations to the approved baseline. For code, use protected branches that require independent approved review before release.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: reviewing change tickets to find unauthorized changes. Tickets only show changes someone recorded; baseline comparison shows what actually changed.

subtopics.name: Patch Management
subtopics.summary: Vendors release patches to fix flaws, many of them security holes. Patches need testing so they do not break production, but every day of delay leaves a known weakness open. Patching is ranked by real risk, with flaws attackers are actively using on exposed systems first. Precise term: patch management, identifying, testing, approving, deploying and verifying vendor fixes on a risk-based schedule.
