illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 524 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Patch management process: identify, test, approve, deploy, verify'><rect x='8' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='54' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Identify</text><rect x='122' y='24' width='70' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='157' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Test</text><rect x='214' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='260' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Approve</text><rect x='328' y='24' width='86' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='371' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Deploy</text><rect x='436' y='24' width='80' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='476' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Verify</text><line x1='102' y1='46' x2='113' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M113,42 L120,46 L113,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='194' y1='46' x2='205' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M205,42 L212,46 L205,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='308' y1='46' x2='319' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M319,42 L326,46 L319,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='416' y1='46' x2='427' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M427,42 L434,46 L427,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: The patch cycle: identify, test, approve, deploy and verify. Testing protects production, but it must not become a reason to leave an exploitable flaw open.

subtopics.key_point: Urgency shortens testing but never removes it. When a patch must wait, use compensating controls and documented, time-bound risk acceptance by the accountable owner.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: ranking patches by severity score alone. Known active exploitation on exposed assets outranks a raw score. Also, internal risk acceptance cannot override an external mandate; use the regulator's formal exception process.

subtopics.name: Release Management
subtopics.summary: A release bundles several approved changes and moves them together into production. Release management plans the bundle, builds it, tests it as a whole and controls the rollout. It promotes the package through a series of environments, each acting as a checkpoint. Precise term: release management, planning, building, testing and deploying a coordinated package of approved changes.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 496 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Release pipeline: development, test, staging, production environments'><rect x='8' y='24' width='116' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='66' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Development</text><rect x='146' y='24' width='90' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='191' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Test</text><rect x='258' y='24' width='100' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='308' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Staging</text><rect x='380' y='24' width='108' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='434' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Production</text><line x1='126' y1='46' x2='137' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M137,42 L144,46 L137,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='238' y1='46' x2='249' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M249,42 L256,46 L249,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='360' y1='46' x2='371' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M371,42 L378,46 L371,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Promotion through environments. A release moves from development to test to staging to production, and staging should look like production so the last check is realistic.

subtopics.key_point: Change management authorizes each individual change; release management coordinates how a group of changes is packaged, tested and rolled out, with a tested rollback.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: treating release management and change management as the same thing. Ask: is the question about approving one change, or coordinating many?

topics.summary: Logs are the record of what happened on a system and who did it. They support troubleshooting, detection and investigations, but only if they are complete, trustworthy and actually reviewed.

subtopics.name: Log Coverage and Retention
subtopics.summary: Each system layer (network, operating system, database, application) keeps its own logs, and a gap at any layer is a blind spot. Logs should tie actions, especially privileged ones, to an individual person. Clocks across systems must agree, or events cannot be put in order. Precise term: log retention, how long each type of log is kept, set by legal, regulatory and business needs.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 450 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Log management: collect logs, store them securely, monitor and analyze them'><rect x='8' y='24' width='84' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='50' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Collect</text><rect x='114' y='24' width='108' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='168' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Store securely</text><rect x='244' y='24' width='88' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='288' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Monitor</text><rect x='354' y='24' width='88' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='398' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Analyze</text><line x1='94' y1='46' x2='105' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M105,42 L112,46 L105,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='224' y1='46' x2='235' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M235,42 L242,46 L235,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='334' y1='46' x2='345' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M345,42 L352,46 L345,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: The log pipeline: collect from every layer, store where they cannot be altered, then monitor and analyze. Skipping the last two steps means the logs detect nothing.

subtopics.key_point: Set retention per log type from legal, regulatory and business requirements, not one uniform period or storage cost. Capture privileged actions by named users, and keep personal or card data out of logs where possible.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: logging only logins. Authentication events do not show what a privileged user did after logging in.

subtopics.name: Protecting and Reviewing Logs
subtopics.summary: A log nobody reads detects nothing, and a log an attacker can edit proves nothing. Logs used as evidence need protection against alteration. Systems also need watching to make sure log sources keep sending and storage does not fill up. Precise term: log integrity, assurance that log records have not been changed or deleted since they were written.

categories.Integrity protection: Hashing or write-once storage, checked periodically.
categories.Segregation: Log administration kept apart from the administrators being logged.
categories.Source health: Alerts when an expected source goes quiet.
categories.Capacity: Thresholds and archiving so logs are not overwritten.

subtopics.key_point: People whose actions are logged must not control those logs. Assign risk-based review with follow-up, alert on changes to logging settings, and suspend scheduled deletion when logs are needed for an inquiry or legal hold.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: "logs are collected and stored, so the control works." Collection is not detection. Also watch for a log source that silently stops reporting; monitoring source health catches it.

topics.summary: Service level management agrees what good service looks like, writes it down in measurable terms, and checks performance against it, for both internal IT and outside providers.

subtopics.name: Service Level Agreements and Metrics
subtopics.summary: A service level agreement (SLA) is a written promise about service, such as hours of availability or how fast tickets are answered. It is only useful if every target can be measured and reported. Good metric sets mix speed with quality and user satisfaction. Precise term: service level agreement (SLA), a documented agreement setting measurable service targets, reporting and remedies.

categories.SLA: Agreement between a service provider and its customer.
categories.OLA: Operational level agreement between internal teams that supports an SLA.
categories.Underpinning contract: Agreement with an outside supplier that supports an SLA.

subtopics.key_point: When money depends on a provider's own figures, measure independently and reconcile to theirs. In a dispute, start from how the contract defines the metric.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: "all SLA targets are green, so service is fine." If users are unhappy while speed targets are met, the metric set is incomplete. Penalties also mean nothing until performance can be measured.

subtopics.name: Service Levels, Architecture and Suppliers
subtopics.summary: A promise of high availability is empty if the systems behind it cannot deliver it, so service targets and system design have to be planned together. With several suppliers, each can meet its own SLA while the end-to-end service still fails. Outsourcing a service does not hand over the business impact. Precise term: end-to-end service level, the performance of the whole transaction path as the user experiences it.
subtopics.key_point: Agreed service levels shape the design and investment, not the other way around. The auditor quantifies gaps and options; management makes the investment decision.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: treating SLA credits as protection. Credits do not transfer business impact; the organization stays accountable for resilience. When relying on a supplier's assurance (SOC) report, first check that its scope and period cover what you are auditing.

topics.summary: Databases hold the organization's records. Auditors look at how data is structured, who can change it, and whether changes are traceable and recoverable.

subtopics.name: Database Models
subtopics.summary: Relational databases store data in tables with fixed columns and enforced relationships, which suits financial transactions. NoSQL databases relax that structure to handle large or varied data at scale. Older hierarchical and network models still run in some legacy systems. Precise term: ACID, the properties that make a transaction reliable: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Relational databases store data in related tables; NoSQL databases handle flexible, unstructured data'><rect x='14' y='18' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Relational</text><line x1='176' y1='39' x2='253' y2='39' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,35 L260,39 L253,43 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='18' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='43' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Tables with set relationships</text><rect x='14' y='66' width='160' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='94' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>NoSQL</text><line x1='176' y1='87' x2='253' y2='87' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M253,83 L260,87 L253,91 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><rect x='262' y='66' width='206' height='42' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='365' y='91' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Flexible, unstructured data</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Two families of databases. Relational stores data in linked tables with a fixed structure; NoSQL gives up some of that structure to handle flexible or unstructured data.

categories.Atomicity: All of a transaction happens or none of it does.
categories.Consistency: Each transaction leaves data in a valid state.
categories.Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other.

subtopics.key_point: Choose the model by workload. When a NoSQL schema is flexible, validation and integrity checks move into the application, so the auditor looks there.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: assuming a plan to replace a legacy database lowers today's risk. Current exposure comes from vendor support and scarce skills now.

subtopics.name: DBMS Structure and the Data Dictionary
subtopics.summary: The database management system (DBMS) is the software that stores, retrieves and protects the data. It keeps a data dictionary, which is data about data: every table, field, type and relationship. Change a definition there and every program that uses it is affected. Precise term: metadata (data dictionary), the stored definitions that describe the database's structure and meaning.
subtopics.key_point: Metadata changes are restricted, logged and version-controlled. Named data stewards own business definitions, and changes go through controlled approval.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: treating conflicting data definitions across reports as a reporting bug. It is a metadata governance gap that needs ownership.

subtopics.name: Database Controls and Administration
subtopics.summary: Database administrators (DBAs) hold very powerful rights, so their work needs extra oversight. Each person should use their own account with only the access they need, so every action traces to a person. Backups must happen often enough to meet the business's data-loss limit. Precise term: least privilege, granting each account only the access its role needs.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Database controls: access controls, encryption, audit trails, backup and recovery'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Access controls</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Encryption</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Audit trails</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Backup and recovery</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Core database controls: access control decides who sees what, encryption protects the data itself, audit trails record changes, and backups make recovery possible.

subtopics.key_point: Those whose activity is logged must not control the logs. If full DBA rights are accepted, compensate with independent, tamper-resistant logging and review of DBA activity.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: shared DBA accounts "for convenience." They make actions untraceable. And backup or replication must run at least as often as the RPO, or the possible data loss exceeds what the business accepted.

topics.summary: The business impact analysis (BIA) is the foundation of all continuity work. It works out which business processes matter most and how quickly harm grows when they stop.

subtopics.name: Purpose, Scope and Ownership
subtopics.summary: A BIA asks, process by process: if this stopped, how bad would it be, and how fast would it get worse? It looks at money, customers, legal and regulatory consequences and reputation. It starts with business processes and only then identifies the systems, people and suppliers each one depends on. Precise term: business impact analysis (BIA), the assessment of the effects of disruption on business processes over time, used to set recovery priorities and objectives.
subtopics.key_point: The BIA measures impact regardless of likelihood; likelihood belongs to the risk assessment. Criticality is a business decision: senior management approves the results, and the auditor advises.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: starting the BIA from the list of IT systems. The unit of analysis is the business process; systems come in later as dependencies. Questionnaire answers should also be validated in interviews or workshops before they are relied on.
common_mistakes: Leaving out reputational or regulatory impact because it is hard to price. Assess it through measurable proxies such as customer loss or regulator scrutiny.
Scoring impact at an average time of year. Use worst-case timing, such as seasonal peaks.

subtopics.name: Recovery Objectives: RTO, RPO, MTD and MBCO
subtopics.summary: The BIA turns impact into concrete targets. One says how much data the business can afford to lose, one says how fast service must be back, and one says the point at which the outage becomes intolerable. Supporting systems must recover at least as fast as the processes that rely on them. Precise term: recovery time objective (RTO), the target time to restore a process after disruption; recovery point objective (RPO), the maximum data loss measured in time.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 148' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='RPO is the data-loss window before a disruption; RTO is the downtime window after it, until service is restored'><line x1='20' y1='80' x2='480' y2='80' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='250' y1='30' x2='250' y2='112' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='250' y='24' text-anchor='middle' font-family='JetBrains Mono, monospace' font-size='7.5' font-weight='700' fill='var(--accent-fill)' letter-spacing='0.08em'>DISRUPTION</text><rect x='40' y='60' width='110' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='95' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Last backup</text><rect x='350' y='60' width='120' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='410' y='84' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Service restored</text><line x1='150' y1='116' x2='248' y2='116' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='252' y1='116' x2='350' y2='116' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='200' y='134' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>RPO — data lost</text><text x='301' y='134' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>RTO — downtime</text></svg>
illustration.caption: RPO and RTO on one timeline. RPO is the stretch between the last good backup and the disruption, the data you lose; RTO is the stretch from the disruption until service is back.

categories.RPO: Maximum tolerable data loss, measured in time before the event.
categories.RTO: Target time to restore service after the event.
categories.MTD: Maximum tolerable downtime; beyond it the business suffers severe or lasting harm.
categories.MBCO: Minimum business continuity objective: the reduced service level acceptable until normal operations return.

subtopics.key_point: Targets come from business impact weighed against cost, not from what IT can currently do. The RTO must sit inside the maximum tolerable downtime, and management approves the targets and accepts residual risk.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: mixing up RTO and RPO. RPO looks backward from the disruption to the last good copy of data; RTO looks forward to when service is restored.
subtopics.memory_aid: RPO = Point in the past (data). RTO = Time to come back (downtime).

topics.summary: Resilience means designing systems and operations so they keep working, perhaps in a reduced way, when parts fail, instead of relying only on recovery afterwards.

subtopics.name: Resilient Technology Design
subtopics.summary: Resilient design removes single points of failure. That includes duplicate disks, servers, network paths and providers, and sites far enough apart that one event cannot hit both. Applications can be built to isolate a failing dependency so the rest keeps working. Precise term: single point of failure, any one component whose failure stops the whole service.

categories.RAID 1 (mirroring): Same data on two disks; survives one disk failure.
categories.Network diversity: Separate providers and physical paths with dynamic routing.
categories.Circuit breaker: Stops calls to a failing dependency so failures do not cascade.
categories.Graceful degradation: Keeps core functions running when parts are unavailable.

subtopics.key_point: Redundancy must be truly independent: separate carriers, physical routes and hazard zones. Prove resilience with controlled fault-injection tests, not design documents.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: treating RAID or replication as a backup. Mirroring protects against a disk failing, but deletion, corruption and ransomware are copied to every disk at once.

subtopics.name: People, Supplier and OT Resilience
subtopics.summary: Technology is not the only thing that fails. A key person can leave, a supplier can go down, and factory or utility systems (operational technology, OT) can stop. Each needs its own fallback. Precise term: operational resilience, the ability to keep delivering critical services through disruption of any resource they depend on.
subtopics.key_point: Fix single-person dependency by building tested capability in another person; documents alone are not enough. Require evidence of critical suppliers' tested recovery, or an alternate source.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: in an OT incident, choosing production or forensics first. Safety of people and the plant comes first; a controlled shutdown outranks keeping the line running.

topics.summary: Backups are the last line of defense against data loss. They only count if they are taken often enough, stored safely away from the original, and proven to restore.

subtopics.name: Backup Schemes and Rotation
subtopics.summary: A full backup copies everything. An incremental backup copies only what changed since the last backup of any kind, and a differential copies everything changed since the last full backup. The choice trades backup time against restore time. Precise term: 3-2-1 rule, keeping three copies of data on two types of media with one copy offsite.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 470 158' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Backup schemes: a full backup copies everything, incremental copies changes since the last backup, differential copies changes since the last full backup'><rect x='14' y='16' width='150' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='89' y='39' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Full</text><rect x='178' y='16' width='278' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='317' y='39' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Copies everything</text><rect x='14' y='60' width='150' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='89' y='83' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Incremental</text><rect x='178' y='60' width='278' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='317' y='83' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Changes since the last backup</text><rect x='14' y='104' width='150' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='89' y='127' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='11' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Differential</text><rect x='178' y='104' width='278' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='317' y='127' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Changes since the last full backup</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Three backup schemes side by side: full copies everything, incremental copies what changed since the last backup, differential copies what changed since the last full backup.

categories.Full: Everything; slowest to take, simplest to restore.
categories.Incremental: Changes since the last backup; fastest to take, longest restore chain.
categories.Differential: Changes since the last full; grows daily, restore needs only two sets.
categories.Grandfather-father-son: Rotation of daily, weekly and monthly media sets for long retention.

subtopics.key_point: Restores from a differential need the full backup plus only the latest differential; incrementals need the full plus every incremental since. Keep at least one immutable or offline copy that ransomware cannot reach.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: mixing up incremental and differential. Ask: changed since the last backup, or since the last full one?

subtopics.name: Offsite Storage and Custody
subtopics.summary: Backups kept in the same building as the systems can be lost in the same fire or flood. Offsite copies must be far enough away, tracked item by item, and accompanied by an up-to-date catalog so the right media can be found fast. In the cloud, the provider runs the infrastructure but the customer still owns its data, keys and proof of restore. Precise term: chain of custody, an itemized, acknowledged record of every handover of backup media.
subtopics.key_point: Offsite storage is useful only if the expected media is really there; prove it with inventory reconciliation. When backups leave the organization, controlling the encryption keys keeps them confidential, even from the provider.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an offsite site in the same region as the primary. One regional event can take out both. Also confirm data residency rules before choosing a cloud backup location; encryption does not change where data resides.

subtopics.name: Restoration and Restore Testing
subtopics.summary: A backup job that says "success" only shows that something was written. The only proof that data can be recovered is restoring it and checking it is complete and correct. Restore tests should be regular and use the stored media itself. Precise term: test restore, recovering data from backup media into a test environment to verify it is usable.
subtopics.key_point: Recoverability is proven by test restores with integrity checks, not by job logs, contracts or creation-time verification.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: "the backup completed without errors" as evidence. It does not prove the data can be restored.

topics.summary: The business continuity plan (BCP) keeps critical business processes running, or restores them, during and after a disruption. It covers people, places, suppliers and technology, not just IT.

subtopics.name: BCP, DRP and the Planning Lifecycle
subtopics.summary: Business continuity covers the whole business: people, premises, suppliers and processes. Disaster recovery is the IT part inside it, focused on getting systems back. The program follows a cycle: management sets policy, the BIA and risk assessment show what matters, strategies are chosen, plans are written, people are trained, plans are tested, and everything is kept current. Precise term: business continuity plan (BCP), the documented procedures for keeping or restoring critical business processes during disruption.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 118' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The business continuity plan is the umbrella; the disaster recovery plan sits inside it, focused on IT systems'><rect x='14' y='20' width='432' height='82' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='var(--accent-fill)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 3'/><text x='230' y='38' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>Business continuity plan (BCP)</text><rect x='70' y='52' width='320' height='38' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='230' y='75' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Disaster recovery plan (DRP)</text></svg>
illustration.caption: BCP and DRP. The business continuity plan is the umbrella for the whole business; the disaster recovery plan sits inside it and focuses on restoring IT.

subtopics.key_point: IT continuity derives from business continuity: the BIA decides what matters and how fast, then IT plans how technology delivers it. The continuity policy is a governance document (mandate, scope, objectives, accountabilities); procedures live in the plans beneath it.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: starting with recovery strategy or site selection before the BIA. Strategy comes after the BIA sets the objectives. People must also be trained before exercises can meaningfully test the plan.
subtopics.memory_aid: Order of the cycle: Policy, Analyze (BIA), Strategize, Plan, Train, Test, Maintain.

subtopics.name: Plan Contents and Decision Authority
subtopics.summary: A plan is useful only if people know who decides what, and when. It names decision-makers for each area with alternates, sets clear criteria for activating the plan, and prepares crisis communications in advance. It also covers reserves of critical supplies and alternate sources. Precise term: delegated authority, the pre-agreed right of a named person or alternate to take continuity decisions within set limits.

categories.Roles and alternates: Named owners per decision area, each with a backup.
categories.Activation criteria: Measurable triggers for declaring a disruption.
categories.Critical supplies: Reserves stored away from the main site, plus an alternate supplier.

subtopics.key_point: Activation must never hinge on one person. Pre-delegate authority with defined criteria so a named alternate can act without delay.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: treating insurance as a continuity strategy. Insurance transfers part of the financial loss but cannot restore operations, customers or reputation. It complements a BCP and never replaces it.

subtopics.name: Maintaining and Auditing the BCP
subtopics.summary: Organizations change all the time, through new systems, acquisitions and staff turnover, and a plan that is not updated drifts out of date. Updates happen on a schedule and also whenever a significant change occurs. Auditors check the plan by tracing from the business's critical processes through to an actual recovery procedure. Precise term: plan maintenance, keeping the BCP current through scheduled and change-triggered reviews and retests.
subtopics.key_point: Completeness is tested by tracing each critical process from the BIA through strategy to a procedure. A stale plan starts with a refreshed BIA, not a rewrite.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: judging readiness by guided walkthroughs. Asking staff to recall roles, triggers and contacts without prompts shows real readiness. Close findings only on evidence the control works, such as a documented test.

topics.summary: The disaster recovery plan (DRP) restores IT systems and data after a serious disruption, within the targets the BIA set. It covers where to recover, who decides, how to do it, and proof that it works.

subtopics.name: Recovery Strategies and Alternate Sites
subtopics.summary: Recovery sites range from an empty room with power (cold) to a fully equipped, current copy of production (hot), with warm in between. A mirrored site keeps data continuously in sync for near-zero loss. Faster sites cost more, so the choice follows the recovery targets. Precise term: alternate processing site, a location prepared in advance to run critical systems when the primary site is unavailable.

categories.Cold site: Space and utilities only; slowest and cheapest.
categories.Warm site: Some equipment and connectivity; data restored at invocation.
categories.Hot site: Fully equipped and ready within hours.
categories.Mirrored site: Continuously synchronized copy; near-zero RTO and RPO.

subtopics.key_point: Choose the cheapest option that still meets the RTO and RPO set by the BIA. Hardware needed to meet an RTO must be pre-arranged, and the site must also meet data residency rules.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: a hot site restored from backups when the RPO is near zero. Restoring from backups still loses data since the last copy; near-zero RPO needs continuous synchronization. On a shared site, the key contract risk is several customers invoking at once.

subtopics.name: Invocation and Recovery Procedures
subtopics.summary: When disaster strikes, someone must decide to switch to recovery mode, quickly and with clear authority. Then the team follows written procedures that a trained alternate could carry out step by step, because the usual experts may be unavailable. Systems come back in an order set by business priority and technical dependencies. Precise term: invocation, the formal decision to activate the disaster recovery plan.
subtopics.key_point: Use measurable invocation criteria and a named authority with a backup. When the criteria are met, that person acts on the playbook without waiting for consensus or later ratification.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: adding up every system's recovery time to get the total. Total recovery time follows the critical path through dependencies, and shared infrastructure such as identity and networking is restored first so critical applications can run.

subtopics.name: Testing the Recovery Plans
subtopics.summary: A plan that has never been tested is a guess. Tests range from reading the plan through, to rehearsing a scenario, to running real workloads at the recovery site, to actually shutting production down. Each test has written scope, objectives and success criteria agreed beforehand. Precise term: parallel test, running critical processing at the recovery site while production keeps running at the primary site.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 538 114' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='BCP test types by thoroughness: checklist is least thorough, full interruption is most thorough'><rect x='8' y='18' width='86' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='51' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Checklist</text><rect x='108' y='18' width='92' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='154' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Walkthrough</text><rect x='214' y='18' width='88' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='258' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Simulation</text><rect x='316' y='18' width='82' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='357' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Parallel</text><rect x='412' y='18' width='118' height='40' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='471' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Full interruption</text><line x1='8' y1='78' x2='521' y2='78' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M521,74 L528,78 L521,82 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><text x='40' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>least thorough</text><text x='490' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='8' font-weight='600' fill='var(--text2)'>most thorough</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Plan tests from least to most thorough: checklist, walkthrough, simulation, parallel and full interruption. Organizations climb this ladder in order; each step adds realism and risk.

subtopics.key_point: A test's value is honest evidence. Continue where safe, record every workaround and failure, give each gap an owner and a date, and confirm the fix in the next test. Prefer system-generated evidence over recollection.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: the full-interruption test as the "best" answer. It is the most thorough but also the riskiest, because it shuts production down; it comes only after simpler tests succeed.

key_terminologies.Availability: The share of agreed service time during which users can actually use a service as required.
key_terminologies.MTBF: Mean time between failures: how long, on average, a component runs before it fails.
key_terminologies.MTTR: Mean time to repair or restore: how long, on average, it takes to get service back after a failure.
key_terminologies.Capacity management: Watching and forecasting resource use so enough capacity is in place before demand arrives.
key_terminologies.CMDB: Configuration management database: a record of IT components, their owners and how they connect.
key_terminologies.Configuration baseline: The approved settings a system must match; live settings are compared against it to spot drift.
key_terminologies.Change management: The process that assesses, approves and records each change before it reaches production.
key_terminologies.Emergency change: An urgent change made through a faster route, reviewed and approved independently soon afterwards.
key_terminologies.Release management: Coordinating, testing and rolling out a package of already-approved changes.
key_terminologies.Patch management: Finding, testing, approving, installing and checking vendor fixes in order of risk.
key_terminologies.Incident: An unplanned interruption or drop in the quality of a service.
key_terminologies.Problem: The unknown underlying cause of one or more incidents.
key_terminologies.Known error: A problem whose cause is understood and has a documented workaround but no permanent fix yet.
key_terminologies.Service level agreement (SLA): A written agreement setting measurable service targets, reporting and remedies.
key_terminologies.End-user computing (EUC): Spreadsheets, scripts and small apps built and run by business users outside IT development.
key_terminologies.Shadow IT: Technology or cloud services used for business without approval from the organization.
key_terminologies.Control totals: Counts or sums compared at both ends of a process to show nothing was lost, added or changed.
key_terminologies.Data dictionary: The database's stored definitions of its tables, fields and relationships (its metadata).
key_terminologies.ACID: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability: the properties of a reliable database transaction.
key_terminologies.Business impact analysis (BIA): A study of how harm grows over time when each business process stops, used to set recovery priorities.
key_terminologies.RPO: Recovery point objective: the most data, measured in time, the business can afford to lose.
key_terminologies.RTO: Recovery time objective: the target time to get a process or system running again after a disruption.
key_terminologies.MTD: Maximum tolerable downtime: the outage length beyond which the business suffers severe or lasting harm.
key_terminologies.MBCO: Minimum business continuity objective: the reduced level of service acceptable until normal operations return.
key_terminologies.Business continuity plan (BCP): Documented arrangements for keeping or restoring critical business processes during disruption.
key_terminologies.Disaster recovery plan (DRP): The IT part of continuity: procedures for restoring systems and data after a serious disruption.
key_terminologies.Hot site: An alternate site fully equipped and ready to take over processing within hours.
key_terminologies.Mirrored site: An alternate site kept continuously in sync with production for near-zero data loss and downtime.
key_terminologies.3-2-1 rule: Keep three copies of data on two kinds of media, with one copy stored offsite.
key_terminologies.Parallel test: A recovery test that runs real processing at the alternate site while production continues normally.

domains.summary: This domain asks how an organization keeps its information safe and what an auditor should look for. Part A covers the protective layers: policies and classification, physical security, identity and access, networks and endpoints, data loss prevention, encryption and PKI, cloud and virtual platforms, and mobile, wireless and connected devices. Part B covers what happens when protection is tested: awareness, attack methods, security testing, monitoring, incident response and forensics. Throughout, the auditor's role is to judge whether controls match the risk and actually operate, then recommend; management decides and owns the risk.
domains.real_life_analogy: Think of how a museum protects its collection. It decides which pieces matter most and how each must be handled (policy and classification). It locks galleries and controls who carries keys (physical and access control), seals valuable items in cases and records who opens them (encryption and logging), and trains staff to spot tricks (awareness). Guards watch cameras and alarms (monitoring), and there is a rehearsed plan for a theft, including protecting the scene for the police (incident response and forensics). No single lock protects the collection; the layers working together do.

topics.topic_name: Information Asset Security Policies, Frameworks, Standards, and Guidelines
topics.summary: Before any lock or tool is chosen, an organization has to decide what it is protecting, how much protection each asset deserves, and who is answerable for it. This topic covers the written rules that set that direction, the outside frameworks that help structure it, and the way data is classified so protection matches value.

subtopics.name: The security document hierarchy
subtopics.summary: Security rules are written at different levels of detail. At the top, a short policy states what leadership expects and who is responsible. Below it, standards set mandatory, measurable requirements; procedures give step-by-step instructions; and guidelines offer advice people may adapt. Precise term: the policy hierarchy (policy, standard, procedure, guideline).

categories.Policy: High-level intent and responsibilities, approved by senior management or the board. Changes rarely.
categories.Standard: Mandatory, specific requirements that put a policy into effect, such as minimum password length.
categories.Procedure: Step-by-step instructions for carrying out a task in line with the standards.

subtopics.key_point: A policy gets its authority from senior management approval and must assign responsibility for protecting information. Authority without named accountability means nobody acts on it.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an answer that criticizes a policy for not naming products or configuration steps. That detail belongs in standards and procedures; a policy should stay technology-neutral. Another trap: treating a guideline as mandatory. If a requirement must be followed, it belongs in a standard.
common_mistakes: Putting product names or settings into the policy itself.
Writing a mandatory rule into a guideline, where people can lawfully ignore it.
Issuing a policy with no review cycle. Policies are reviewed on a set schedule and whenever a major change, such as a new law, makes them outdated.

subtopics.name: Frameworks and certifiable standards
subtopics.summary: Frameworks give an organization a ready-made structure for its security program so it does not start from a blank page. Some, such as ISO/IEC 27001, define a management system that an accredited body can certify. Others, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, are voluntary and describe outcomes to aim for. Precise term: a control framework (certifiable standard versus voluntary outcome-based framework).

categories.ISO/IEC 27001: Requirements for an information security management system (ISMS). Certifiable, but only for the scope stated on the certificate.
categories.ISO/IEC 27002: Guidance on implementing security controls. Not certifiable on its own.
categories.NIST CSF 2.0: Voluntary, outcome-based framework with six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Uses profiles (current and target) and tiers.
categories.COBIT: Governance and management framework for enterprise IT, including security-related objectives.

subtopics.key_point: Controls are chosen to treat the organization's assessed risks. A framework is a reference and a checklist of ideas, not a replacement for the risk assessment. Pick a framework by first listing binding legal, regulatory and contractual requirements.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: assuming NIST CSF Implementation Tiers are maturity levels. Tiers describe how rigorous and risk-informed the cybersecurity risk management practices are; they are not a maturity score to climb for its own sake. Also remember CSF 2.0 has six functions, with Govern added to Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
common_mistakes: Trusting a vendor's ISO 27001 certificate without checking that the service you use is inside its scope.
Accepting a Statement of Applicability that excludes controls with no risk-based justification.
Running each framework's audit separately instead of mapping one common control set to all of them, so each control is tested once.
subtopics.memory_aid: CSF 2.0 functions: "Good Ideas Protect Data, Respond, Recover" for Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

subtopics.name: Security baselines and exceptions
subtopics.summary: A baseline is the minimum security setup every system of a given type must meet, such as patches applied, unneeded services disabled and logging on. It is a floor, not a goal. Baselines drift as people make changes, so they need regular scanning to stay true. Precise term: a security configuration baseline (for example, one based on CIS Benchmarks).
subtopics.key_point: When a system cannot meet the baseline, the gap goes through a formal exception: documented, risk-accepted by the asset owner, given an expiry date, and backed by a compensating control that is verified as working.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an exception that was approved once and never revisited. Risk acceptances hold only for the conditions assessed, so they need expiry and reassessment. Also watch for an overall compliance rate that hides failures on the most critical systems; weight results by asset criticality.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='A security baseline: latest patches, antivirus active, unneeded services off, hardened configuration'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Latest patches</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Antivirus active</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Unneeded services off</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Hardened configuration</text></svg>
illustration.caption: A baseline lists the minimum settings every system of a given type must have. Systems may go further, never below it without an approved exception.

subtopics.name: Roles, ownership and classification
subtopics.summary: Every important data set needs one person who answers for it. That data owner, usually a business manager, decides how sensitive the data is and who may use it. IT staff then apply the protection the owner asked for. A single classification scheme, with handling rules for each level, lets every team protect data the same way. Precise terms: data owner, data custodian, data classification.

categories.Data owner: Business manager accountable for the data. Sets classification and approves access.
categories.Data custodian: Runs the systems and applies the owner's requirements: backups, access settings, encryption.
categories.Data user: Uses the data for approved work and follows the handling rules.
categories.Security function: Advises, sets standards and monitors. Does not own business data.

subtopics.key_point: Data owners classify data and approve access; custodians (such as system administrators) implement and operate the controls. Accountability stays with the owner even when the work is delegated.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an option that has the IT department or the security team decide who gets access to business data. The owner decides; IT implements. Another trap: each business unit inventing its own labels, which breaks consistent handling.

subtopics.name: Privacy principles and acceptable use
subtopics.summary: Security protects data from misuse; privacy decides what personal data may be collected and how it may be used at all. Common principles include collecting only what a stated purpose needs, not reusing data for unrelated purposes, and honoring people's rights to see their data. Separately, an acceptable use policy tells everyone who uses company systems what they may and may not do. Precise terms: privacy principles (such as purpose limitation and data minimization) and the acceptable use policy (AUP).
subtopics.key_point: Privacy rules limit the purpose, not just the access. Under laws such as the GDPR, data collected for one purpose cannot simply be reused for a new, incompatible one, and data should not be collected for an undefined future use.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: assuming encryption makes a cross-border transfer of personal data lawful. Encryption protects the data in transit, but the transfer still needs a legal basis, such as an adequacy decision or standard contractual clauses. Also, an AUP applies to contractors and temporary staff too, and each user should acknowledge it.

topics.summary: Logical controls mean little if someone can walk off with the server or a burst pipe can flood it. This topic covers protection against environmental hazards and against unauthorized people reaching equipment and media.

subtopics.name: Environmental hazards and controls
subtopics.summary: Computer rooms face heat, humidity, water, fire and power problems. Each hazard needs a matching control, such as cooling, water sensors, fire suppression and backup power, plus an alarm that reaches someone who can act in time. Precise term: environmental controls.

categories.Fire: Detection (smoke, heat), suppression (clean-agent gas for occupied rooms; pre-action sprinklers as the preferred water option), extinguishers, and trained staff.
categories.Water: Raised floors, under-floor water sensors, no water pipes above equipment where avoidable.
categories.Power: UPS for short gaps and clean power; generator for long outages; surge protection.
categories.Temperature and humidity: Dedicated cooling, monitoring with alerts, redundant HVAC for critical rooms.

subtopics.key_point: A sensor protects nothing unless its alert reaches a person who can respond before damage occurs. Monitoring and response are part of the control, not extras.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an answer that relies on a UPS alone for a long outage. Batteries only bridge short gaps and the generator start-up; only a generator with fuel keeps a site running for hours. If power loss cannot be avoided, an orderly shutdown protects data integrity.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 460 132' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Environmental threats a data center must control: fire, flooding, power failure, temperature'><rect x='14' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Fire</text><rect x='236' y='16' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='42' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Flooding</text><rect x='14' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='119' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Power failure</text><rect x='236' y='74' width='210' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--surface)' stroke='var(--border2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='341' y='100' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='10' font-weight='700' fill='var(--text)'>Temperature</text></svg>
illustration.caption: Four hazards every data center must plan for. Each needs its own detection, its own control and a person who acts on the alarm.

subtopics.name: Physical access controls
subtopics.summary: Physical security works in rings: the site perimeter, the building entrance, then the most sensitive rooms. Each ring should admit fewer people than the one outside it. Badge systems tie each entry to one person and can be switched off quickly when someone leaves. Precise terms: defense in depth for physical security, least privilege for physical zones.

categories.Deterrent: Signs, lighting, visible cameras. Discourage an attempt.
categories.Preventive: Locks, badge readers, mantraps, fences. Stop an entry.
categories.Detective: Alarms, CCTV review, access logs. Reveal an entry after it happens.

subtopics.key_point: Physical access follows least privilege, just like system access: badges open only the areas a role needs. Rights must be reviewed against current HR records so leavers and movers lose access.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: a choice that adds a guard or sign when the question asks for the BEST preventive control against tailgating. A mantrap (airlock) that admits one person per authentication enforces the rule; awareness training supports it. Also, CCTV footage only works as evidence if the people being watched cannot alter or delete it.
common_mistakes: Giving cleaning or maintenance crews badges that open every area.
Logging visitors without prior approval by a named host, an escort and a distinct badge.
Testing only the badge list, instead of comparing it with an authoritative source such as current HR data.

illustration.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 352 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Layered physical security: perimeter, building entry, then the server room — control tightens at each layer'><rect x='8' y='24' width='92' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='54' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Perimeter</text><rect x='122' y='24' width='104' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='174' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Building entry</text><rect x='248' y='24' width='96' height='44' rx='4' fill='var(--accent-fill)'/><text x='296' y='50' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Plus Jakarta Sans, Segoe UI, sans-serif' font-size='9.5' font-weight='700' fill='#ffffff'>Server room</text><line x1='102' y1='46' x2='113' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M113,42 L120,46 L113,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/><line x1='228' y1='46' x2='239' y2='46' stroke='var(--text2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M239,42 L246,46 L239,50 Z' fill='var(--text2)'/></svg>
illustration.caption: Control tightens as you move inward. Fewer people pass each ring, and the server room should admit only those whose job needs it.

topics.summary: Identity and access management (IAM) makes sure each person or system is who it claims to be, can do only what it needs, and leaves a trail. This topic covers authentication, authorization, access models, the joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle, privileged access and zero trust.

subtopics.name: Authentication, authorization and accountability
subtopics.summary: Getting into a system involves three separate questions. Are you really who you say? What are you allowed to do? And can we trace what you did back to you? Each step depends on the one before it. Precise terms: authentication, authorization, accountability (the three As).

categories.Possession: Something you have: hardware key, phone app, smart card.

subtopics.key_point: Accountability needs unique identities. Shared or generic accounts break it, because logs show the account, not the person behind it.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: confusing multi-factor with multi-step. A password plus a security question is still one factor (two things you know). Real MFA mixes categories: something you know, something you have, something you are.
common_mistakes: Mixing up the biometric error rates. The false acceptance rate (FAR) counts impostors let in, a security failure. The false rejection rate (FRR) counts genuine users turned away, an inconvenience.
Assuming any MFA stops phishing. Codes can be relayed through a fake site; phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 keys are bound to the genuine site.
Treating knowledge-based questions as strong identity proofing. They give weak assurance.

subtopics.name: Access control models
subtopics.summary: Organizations decide access in different ways. Sometimes the owner of a file decides; sometimes the system enforces fixed labels nobody can override; usually access follows the job role; and increasingly it depends on attributes checked at the moment of the request. Precise terms: DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC.

categories.DAC (discretionary): The resource owner grants access at their discretion. Flexible, hard to control.
categories.MAC (mandatory): The system enforces classification labels and clearances. Rigid, strong.
categories.RBAC (role-based): Access comes from the job role. Common in business; simplifies reviews.
categories.ABAC (attribute-based): Each request is checked against subject, resource and environment attributes, so access changes as those attributes change.

subtopics.key_point: Least privilege and segregation of duties apply whatever the model: give only what the task needs, and make sure no one person can complete a sensitive process alone.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: thinking a data owner can override a mandatory access control label. Under MAC, the system enforces labels and clearances, and individual users, owners included, cannot change them. Another trap: relying on after-the-fact log review instead of segregation of duties. Detective reviews are a fallback, not a substitute.

subtopics.name: The identity lifecycle
subtopics.summary: People join, change jobs and leave, and their access has to follow. When someone moves to a new role, their old rights must be removed, not just new ones added. Business owners should regularly confirm that each person still needs what they have. Precise terms: joiner-mover-leaver process and access recertification.
subtopics.key_point: Access recertification should be risk-tiered: privileged access reviewed more often, and reviewed by people who understand the business need. Without it, excess access quietly piles up.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an answer that disables a user at the central identity provider and assumes all access ends. In federated setups (SAML, OIDC), applications keep their own sessions, which continue unless revocation is handled. Also, every service account needs a named owner, or nobody can recertify or retire it.
common_mistakes: Movers keeping old rights after a transfer ("privilege creep").
Leavers whose accounts stay active because HR and IT are not linked.
Reviews done by IT staff who cannot judge the business need.

subtopics.name: Privileged access management
subtopics.summary: Administrator accounts can change or erase almost anything, so they are the top target for attackers. Good practice removes always-on admin rights. Instead, people request elevated access, someone else approves it, and it is granted for a short recorded session before expiring. Precise terms: privileged access management (PAM) and just-in-time (JIT) access.
subtopics.key_point: JIT access depends on independent approval. If requesters can approve themselves, time limits alone cannot stop misuse. Admins should also use separate privileged accounts and avoid signing in to ordinary workstations with them.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: thinking a password reset ends an active attacker's access. Issued sessions and tokens may stay valid; containment means disabling the account and revoking its sessions. For a leaked privileged credential, assume compromise and rotate it immediately.

subtopics.name: Zero trust
subtopics.summary: The old model trusted anyone inside the corporate network. Zero trust drops that assumption: every request is checked using who the user is, the health of their device and the context, wherever it comes from. Trust is re-checked during the session, not granted once. Precise term: zero trust architecture (described in NIST SP 800-207).
subtopics.key_point: Zero trust means each request is authorized by policy. Proving identity alone is not enough; a policy must still decide what that identity may reach right now.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: equating zero trust with buying one product, or with MFA alone. It is an architecture of continuous, policy-based decisions. Another trap: a service mesh that authenticates services but then lets any authenticated service call any other. That is implicit trust in a new form.

topics.summary: Networks carry data between systems and endpoints are where people actually touch it. This topic covers filtering and segmenting traffic, detecting and blocking attacks on the wire, and hardening the laptops, servers and phones at the edges.

subtopics.name: Firewalls and web application firewalls
subtopics.summary: A firewall decides which traffic may pass between network zones. Simple ones look only at addresses and ports; more advanced ones track connections and inspect the content of applications. A web application firewall (WAF) sits in front of a website and blocks attacks such as SQL injection. Precise terms: packet-filtering, stateful, proxy and next-generation firewalls; WAF.
subtopics.key_point: A firewall is only as good as its rule set and the change control around it. Rules should default to deny, be approved through change management and be reviewed regularly.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: a WAF left in monitoring mode. It only prevents attacks in blocking mode; monitoring is for tuning first. Another trap: treating a WAF as the fix for SQL injection. It is a compensating layer (virtual patching); the real fix is parameterized queries in the code.

subtopics.name: Segmentation and the screened subnet
subtopics.summary: Splitting a network into zones stops one compromised machine from reaching everything. Internet-facing servers go in a screened subnet (often called a DMZ) between two layers of filtering, and sensitive internal systems sit in their own segments. Microsegmentation applies the same idea down to individual workloads. Precise terms: network segmentation, screened subnet (DMZ), microsegmentation.
subtopics.key_point: Segmentation limits lateral movement only while its rules stay tight. Rule changes need change control; one unapproved "allow any" rule quietly undoes it.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: redesigning segments before mapping the environment and data flows. You must know where sensitive data (for example, cardholder data) travels before you can draw sensible zones. Guest Wi-Fi belongs on its own segment that reaches only the internet.

subtopics.name: Intrusion detection, prevention and access control
subtopics.summary: An intrusion detection system (IDS) watches traffic and raises alerts. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) can also block bad traffic, but only if the traffic actually flows through it. Network access control (NAC) checks a device before letting it join the network. Precise terms: IDS, IPS, NAC; unified threat management (UTM) for an appliance that bundles several of these.
subtopics.key_point: An IPS must sit inline to block. Connected to a mirrored port, it can only see and alert. NAC should check device health, not just the user's credentials, and quarantine devices that fail.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: assuming a bundled UTM appliance removes the need for redundancy. It concentrates several controls in one box, which is simpler but becomes a single point of failure.

subtopics.name: Endpoint protection and hardening
subtopics.summary: Every laptop, server and phone is a possible way in. Endpoints are protected in layers: a hardened configuration, prompt patching, disk encryption, a host firewall, and software that spots malicious behavior. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) watches what processes do, so it can catch attacks that use legitimate built-in tools and leave no malware file. Precise terms: endpoint hardening, EDR.
subtopics.key_point: Coverage comes first. A device without the agent sends no data, so a clean console can overstate protection. Confirm the population of covered devices before trusting the results.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: assuming full-disk encryption on laptops protects copies on USB drives. Encryption has to follow the data onto every portable medium. Also, hardening decays; configuration scans detect drift from the baseline.

topics.summary: Data loss prevention (DLP) tools look for sensitive data leaving where it should stay, whether by email, web upload, USB drive or cloud share, and alert or block. This topic covers what DLP protects, how it recognizes sensitive data, and how to roll it out without breaking the business.

subtopics.name: What DLP covers
subtopics.summary: Sensitive data exists in three states: stored, moving across a network, and open on someone's screen. DLP comes in matching forms: network DLP watches traffic, endpoint DLP controls actions on the device (including USB and printing, even off the corporate network), and discovery DLP scans storage to find where sensitive data sits. Precise terms: data at rest, in motion and in use; network, endpoint and discovery DLP.
subtopics.key_point: DLP cannot protect data nobody has identified. Data discovery and owner-led classification come before enforcement rules.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: a DLP deployment that ignores the channel where data actually leaves. Network DLP also cannot read encrypted traffic; governed TLS inspection at the proxy restores that visibility.

subtopics.name: Detecting sensitive data
subtopics.summary: DLP recognizes sensitive content in different ways. Pattern rules look for shapes such as card numbers; exact data matching compares content with fingerprints of real records; and context rules consider who is sending what, to whom, over which channel. Combining content and context lets normal work through and stops leaks. Precise terms: pattern matching, exact data matching (EDM), contextual analysis.
subtopics.key_point: Move a DLP rule from monitor mode to blocking only after its false positive rate has been measured and is acceptable. Then block, not just alert, where the business case allows.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: a senior executive whose blocked transfer is waved through. If an approved secure channel existed, the policy breach is enforced; seniority does not create an exception.
common_mistakes: Turning on blocking on day one and flooding the business with false positives.
Leaving rules in alert-only mode forever.
Monitoring employees in several countries without a legal basis and policy for each one.

subtopics.name: Auditing DLP effectiveness
subtopics.summary: To know whether DLP works, an auditor wants more than the vendor's dashboard. The strongest evidence is a test the auditor runs, such as sending seeded test records through each channel and checking they are caught. When DLP finds sensitive data in the wrong place, access is restricted first, and the data owner decides what happens next. Precise term: re-performance (evidence the auditor generates).
subtopics.key_point: Evidence the auditor generates by testing is more reliable than counts, claims or confirmations from the people who run the tool.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: accepting the number of alerts as proof the control works. Alert counts show activity, not effectiveness. A finding of personal data in a test environment may itself be a breach that needs containment and a notification assessment.

topics.summary: Encryption turns readable data into scrambled data that only a key holder can restore. This topic covers the two main kinds of encryption, hashing, digital signatures, and the key management that decides whether any of it actually protects anything.

subtopics.name: Symmetric encryption
subtopics.summary: Symmetric encryption uses one secret key to both lock and unlock data. It is fast, so it is used for large volumes, such as whole disks, databases and network sessions. Its weakness is distribution: both sides need the same key, and every pair of parties needs its own. Precise term: symmetric (secret-key) cryptography, for example AES.
subtopics.key_point: The algorithm is rarely the weak point; the key is. Strong encryption with a badly protected key gives little protection.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: an option using AES in ECB mode. Identical input blocks produce identical output, so patterns leak. An authenticated mode such as GCM hides patterns and also detects tampering.

subtopics.name: Asymmetric encryption
subtopics.summary: Asymmetric encryption uses a matched pair of keys. The public key can be shared with anyone; the private key stays with its owner. What one key locks, only the other can unlock. It is much slower than symmetric encryption, so in practice it is used to exchange a symmetric key safely, and the symmetric key then encrypts the data. Precise term: asymmetric (public-key) cryptography, for example RSA or elliptic-curve.
subtopics.key_point: Use asymmetric cryptography to exchange keys and to sign; use symmetric cryptography for bulk data. Each covers the other's weakness. Asymmetric also scales: one key pair per party replaces a secret key for every pair of parties.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: mixing up which key does what. To send something confidential, encrypt with the recipient's public key. To prove you sent it, sign with your own private key. Also note "harvest now, decrypt later": long-lived secrets sent today with current public-key methods are the first priority for post-quantum migration, which starts with a cryptographic inventory.

subtopics.name: Hashing, salting and tokenization
subtopics.summary: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint, and you cannot run it backward. Changing even one character changes the fingerprint, so hashes show whether data was altered. Passwords should be stored as salted, deliberately slow hashes, so they can be checked but not recovered. Tokenization swaps a sensitive value, such as a card number, for a meaningless stand-in and keeps the real value in a secured vault. Precise terms: cryptographic hash, salt, tokenization.

categories.Hashing: One-way. Used for integrity checks and password storage.
categories.Encryption: Two-way with the right key. Used for confidentiality.
categories.Tokenization: Replaces the value with a token; the real value can be recovered only through the vault.

subtopics.key_point: Hashing gives integrity, not confidentiality. A hash used for integrity must resist collisions; MD5 and SHA-1 no longer qualify.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: storing passwords with fast, unsalted hashes. A unique salt per password defeats precomputed rainbow tables. And remember tokenization shrinks PCI DSS scope because most systems never hold the real card number.

subtopics.name: Digital signatures
subtopics.summary: A digital signature proves who sent a message and that it was not changed. The sender creates a hash of the message and signs it with their private key. The receiver checks the signature with the sender's public key and compares it with a fresh hash of what arrived. If they match, the message is authentic and intact. Precise terms: digital signature, providing integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.
subtopics.key_point: A signature is only as trustworthy as the custody of the signing key. If many people or systems can reach the key, anyone could sign malicious code in the company's name.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: thinking a digital signature keeps the message secret. It does not; the content stays readable unless it is also encrypted. Signatures give integrity, origin authentication and non-repudiation, not confidentiality.

subtopics.name: Key management
subtopics.summary: Keys have a life: they are generated, distributed, stored, used, rotated, archived and finally destroyed. Each key should have a set lifetime (cryptoperiod) based on what it protects. High-value keys belong in tamper-resistant hardware called a hardware security module (HSM). Precise term: cryptographic key management lifecycle.
subtopics.key_point: Separate key control from data control. To protect data from database administrators, keep the keys outside their control. Critical key operations need dual control and split knowledge, so no single person can export a key.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: destroying a key before the data it protects has reached the end of its retention period, which makes that data unrecoverable for good. Another: rotating a key to fix excess access. If the same people can still decrypt, fix the permission grant instead.
common_mistakes: Keeping keys in source code or configuration files.
No defined cryptoperiod, so keys are never rotated.
Releasing a recovered key without verifying who is asking for it.

topics.summary: Public-key encryption only helps if you can trust that a public key really belongs to who it claims. Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the system of authorities, certificates and rules that provides that trust. This topic covers its parts, the certificate lifecycle and what can go wrong.

subtopics.name: PKI components and the chain of trust
subtopics.summary: A certificate is a signed statement binding a public key to a name. A certificate authority (CA) signs it, after a registration authority (RA) checks the requester's identity. CAs are arranged in a chain: a root CA, kept offline, signs intermediate CAs, which issue everyday certificates. Software trusts a certificate by tracing it back to a root it already trusts. Precise terms: certificate authority, registration authority, certification practice statement (CPS), chain of trust.

categories.Root CA: Top of the chain. Self-signed, offline, used rarely.
categories.Intermediate (subordinate) CA: Issues certificates day to day; can be revoked without replacing the root.
categories.Registration authority: Verifies the identity of requesters before the CA issues.
categories.Certificate revocation list / OCSP: Ways to publish and check which certificates are no longer trusted.

subtopics.key_point: A certificate is only as trustworthy as the identity check behind it. Before relying on an outside PKI, review its certification practice statement for identity proofing, key protection and revocation.
subtopics.exam_tip: Trap: keeping the root CA online for convenience. An offline root, with its key in an HSM under dual control, protects the trust anchor; online subordinate CAs handle routine issuance.
